name: 1 Samuel
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where 1 Samuel is called 1 Kingdoms) and against the Dead Sea Scrolls of Samuel, chiefly 4QSam-a, the largest of them. In Samuel the traditional Hebrew text has suffered more copying damage than in most books, and the Septuagint and 4QSam-a often preserve an older or fuller wording; the most important differences are footnoted (for example, the Nahash paragraph before chapter 11, the short Greek text of chapters 17–18, Goliath’s height, the Song of Hannah, and the gap in 13:1). Every Septuagint reading cited in the footnotes was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation (quoted in modernized wording). Readings of the Dead Sea Scrolls are stated in general terms (“is reported to read”) until they can be checked against the critical editions. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (20:42; 23:29; 24:1–22), a footnote says so. Measurements are given in modern US units, and times and dates use modern equivalents, with the originals in the footnotes.

verses.text: There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim,{a} in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah{b} son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. One was named Hannah{c} and the other Peninnah.{d} Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.

This man used to go up from his town every year to bow down and to sacrifice to Yahweh{e} of Armies{f} at Shiloh,{g} and the two sons of Eli,{h} Hophni{i} and Phinehas,{j} were priests of Yahweh there.
On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he gave shares of the meat to Peninnah his wife and to each of her sons and daughters,
but to Hannah he gave a double share,{k} for it was Hannah he loved, though Yahweh had shut up her womb.
Her rival would taunt her bitterly to provoke her, because Yahweh had closed her womb.
So it went on year after year. Every time Hannah went up to the house of Yahweh, her rival provoked her, and she wept and would not eat.
Her husband Elkanah would say to her, “Hannah, why are you crying? Why will you not eat? Why is your heart so sad? Am I not worth more to you than ten sons?”
Once, after they had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah got up.{l} Eli the priest was sitting on his seat beside the doorpost of the temple of Yahweh.
Deeply distressed, she prayed to Yahweh and wept bitterly.

She made a vow and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will truly look on the misery of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but give your servant a male child, then I will give him to Yahweh for all the days of his life, and no razor will ever touch his head.”{m}
As she kept on praying before Yahweh, Eli was watching her mouth.
Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips were moving, and her voice could not be heard. So Eli supposed she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you go on being drunk? Get rid of your wine.”
But Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor beer. I have been pouring out my soul before Yahweh.
Do not count your servant as a worthless woman,{n} for all this time I have been speaking out of my great anguish and grief.”
Then Eli answered, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant what you have asked of him.”
She said, “Let your servant find favor in your sight.” Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer downcast.{o}
They rose early in the morning and bowed down before Yahweh; then they went back home to Ramah. Elkanah knew his wife Hannah, and Yahweh remembered her.
In due time Hannah conceived and bore a son. She named him Samuel,{p} saying, “Because I asked Yahweh for him.”
Then Elkanah went up, he and his whole household, to offer Yahweh the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow.
But Hannah did not go up. She told her husband, “Not until the child is weaned. Then I will take him, and he will appear before Yahweh and stay there for good.”{q}

Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Do whatever you think is good. Wait here until you have weaned him. Only may Yahweh confirm his word.”{r} So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.

When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull,{s} about three-fifths of a bushel of flour,{t} and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of Yahweh at Shiloh. The child was still young.
Then they slaughtered the bull and took the boy to Eli.
She said, “Excuse me, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am that woman who was standing near you here, praying to Yahweh.
For this child I prayed, and Yahweh has granted me what I asked of him.
So I in turn have lent him to Yahweh.{u} For as long as he lives he is lent to Yahweh.” And he{v} worshiped Yahweh there.

notes.text: Ramathaim-zophim means “two heights of the Zuphites” (compare “Zuph” later in the verse). The town is called Ramah, “height,” in verse 19. The Septuagint reads “Armathaim Zipha” (Brenton, “Armathaim Sipha”); its exact site is uncertain.
Elkanah means “God has created” or “God has acquired.” The Septuagint spells the names in this genealogy differently (Brenton: Helkana, Jeremeel, Elius, Thocca, Suph).
Hannah means “grace” or “favor.” The Septuagint spells it “Anna.”
Peninnah may mean “coral” or “pearl” (uncertain).
Yahweh is the personal name of Israel’s God (Hebrew YHWH), which many English versions replace with “the LORD.” This translation writes the name.

Hebrew Yahweh tsebaʾot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts” (or “Yahweh Sabaoth”). The armies may be Israel’s forces, the heavenly host, or both. This is the first time the title appears in the Bible; it occurs often in Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The Septuagint keeps the Hebrew word: “Lord God of Sabaoth” (Brenton, 1:11).
Shiloh, where the tent of meeting stood in this period (Joshua 18:1), is about 20 miles (30 kilometers) north of Jerusalem; the name may mean “place of rest” (uncertain).
Eli probably means “exalted” or “my God” (uncertain).
Hophni is probably an Egyptian name, perhaps “tadpole” (uncertain).
Phinehas is an Egyptian name meaning “the Nubian.”

The Hebrew is difficult. Literally “one portion of two faces,” perhaps “a double portion” or “a choice portion”; some take it to mean “only one portion.” The Septuagint reads “a prime portion, because she had no child” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds, “and stood before the Lord” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds, “and he will drink no wine or strong drink” (Brenton, modernized). Compare the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6:1–8 and Samson in Judges 13:5.
Hebrew “a daughter of Belial,” an expression for a worthless or wicked person.
The Septuagint reads, “and entered into her lodging, and ate and drank with her husband” (Brenton, modernized).

Samuel (Hebrew Shemuʾel) probably means “name of God” or “heard by God.” Hannah’s explanation is a wordplay on the verb shaʾal, “to ask,” which is the root of the name Saul (Shaʾul). The pun may hint at the story of Saul, the king Israel “asked for” (8:10; 12:13).
Or “for all time.” 4QSam-a is reported to add that she would dedicate him as a Nazirite for all time (compare verse 11).
So the traditional Hebrew text (MT). The Septuagint reads “may the Lord establish that which comes out of your mouth” (Brenton, modernized), and 4QSam-a is reported to agree with the Greek.

So the Septuagint (Brenton, “a calf of three years old”), 4QSam-a (as reported), and other ancient witnesses. The traditional Hebrew text reads “with three bulls,” but verse 25 mentions only one bull; dividing the Hebrew letters differently gives “a three-year-old bull.”
Hebrew “an ephah of flour,” a dry measure of about 22 liters.
Hebrew shaʾul, “asked” or “lent,” the same form as the name Saul. The verse plays on the root “ask” used in verses 17, 20, and 27.
That is, Elkanah, or possibly Samuel. Some Hebrew manuscripts read “they.” The Septuagint instead reads “and she said” (Brenton) and goes straight into Hannah’s song.

verses.text: Then Hannah prayed and said,{a} “My heart exults in Yahweh; my horn{b} is raised high in Yahweh.{c} My mouth gapes wide against my enemies, for I take joy in your rescue.
No one is holy like Yahweh; indeed, there is no one besides you, and there is no rock like our God.{d}
Stop piling up proud words; let no arrogance come from your mouth, for Yahweh is a God who knows, and by him actions are weighed.{e}
The bows of the mighty are broken, while those who stumbled are wrapped in strength.
Those who had plenty now hire themselves out for bread, while the hungry hunger no more.{f} The childless woman has borne seven, but the mother of many pines away.
Yahweh puts to death and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol{g} and raises up.
Yahweh makes poor and makes rich; he humbles, and he also exalts.

He lifts the poor from the dust; from the ash heap he raises the needy, to seat them with nobles and give them a throne of honor as their inheritance. For the pillars of the earth belong to Yahweh, and on them he has set the world.{h}
He guards the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked are silenced in darkness, for no one prevails by strength.

Yahweh shatters those who oppose him;{i} against them he thunders from the heavens. Yahweh judges the ends of the earth. He gives strength to his king and raises high the horn of his anointed one.”{j}
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy remained to serve Yahweh in the presence of Eli the priest.{k}
But the sons of Eli were worthless men;{l} they had no regard for Yahweh
or the priests’ rightful due from the people.{m} Whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant would come while the meat was boiling, holding a three-pronged fork,
and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. Whatever the fork brought up, the priest took for himself. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh.

What is more, even before they burned the fat, the priest’s servant used to come and tell the man offering the sacrifice, “Hand over meat for the priest to roast. He will not accept boiled meat from you, only raw.”
And if the man answered him, “The fat must be burned first; after that, take as much as you like,” he would reply, “No, you will hand it over now, and if not, I will take it by force.”
So the young men’s sin was very great in Yahweh’s sight, for the men treated Yahweh’s offering with contempt.
But Samuel was serving before Yahweh, a boy dressed in a linen ephod.{n}
Every year his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, “May Yahweh give you offspring from this woman in exchange for the one she asked for and lent to Yahweh.”{o} Then they would return home.
Yahweh visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grew up before Yahweh.
Eli was very old. He kept hearing about everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.{p}
He said to them, “Why do you do such things? From all these people I hear reports of your wicked deeds.
No, my sons. What I hear Yahweh’s people spreading about you is not a good report.

If one person sins against another, God{q} may mediate for him; but if someone sins against Yahweh, who can plead for him?” But they would not listen to their father, for it was Yahweh’s will to put them to death.
Meanwhile the boy Samuel kept growing, both in stature and in favor with Yahweh and with people.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Did I not reveal myself plainly to your father’s house when they were in Egypt, slaves to Pharaoh’s house?{r}

Out of all the tribes of Israel I chose him to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to carry the ephod before me. I gave your father’s house all the food offerings of the Israelites.
Why then do you trample{s} on my sacrifices and on the offerings I ordered for my dwelling? Why do you honor your sons above me, growing fat on the best part of every offering of Israel my people?’

Therefore Yahweh, the God of Israel, declares: ‘I did say that your house and your father’s house would walk before me forever.’ But now Yahweh declares: ‘Far be it from me! Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be treated as nothing.
Look, days are coming when I will cut off your arm{t} and the arm of your father’s house, until there is no old man left in your house.
You will look with envy on all the good that is done for Israel,{u} and never will there be an old man in your house.
Any of yours whom I do not cut off from my altar will be spared only to wear out your{v} eyes and grieve your heart, and all the increase of your house will die as men in their prime.{w}
And what happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will be the sign to you: on one day both of them will die.
I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act in keeping with what is in my heart and mind. I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed one forever.

Whoever is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a small silver coin{x} or a loaf of bread, and will say, “Please assign me to one of the priestly duties, so that I can have a scrap of bread to eat.”’”

notes.text: The Song of Hannah (2:1–10) is a poem of praise for God who reverses human fortunes; compare Mary’s song in Luke 1:46–55. The Septuagint and 4QSam-a differ from the traditional Hebrew text in several lines, as noted below. This needs scholarly review.
The horn is an image of strength and dignity, taken from the horns of a wild ox.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “in my God” (Brenton), and some Hebrew manuscripts are reported to agree.
The Septuagint reads “For there is none holy as the Lord, and there is none righteous as our God: there is none holy besides you” (Brenton, modernized), without the line about the rock.
Or “and actions are not weighed,” following the written Hebrew (ketiv), which has “not” rather than “by him.” The Septuagint reads “and God prepares his own designs” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew uncertain; literally “and the hungry cease.” The Septuagint reads “and the hungry have forsaken the land” (Brenton).
Sheol is the realm of the dead (the grave, the underworld).

The Septuagint lacks these two lines and instead reads, “granting his request to the one who prays; and he blesses the years of the righteous” (Brenton, modernized), at the start of verse 9; it also lacks the first two lines of verse 9 as they stand in Hebrew. 4QSam-a is reported to agree with the Greek here in part.

So the Hebrew as traditionally read (qere); the written text (ketiv) has the singular, “the one who contends with him.” The Septuagint reads, “The Lord will weaken his adversary; the Lord is holy” (Brenton).

Hebrew mashiaḥ, “anointed one,” from which the title “Messiah” comes. In the Septuagint, this verse is much longer. After “the Lord is holy” it adds, in words close to Jeremiah 9:23–24: “Let the wise man not boast in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his strength, nor the rich man in his wealth; but let the one who boasts boast in this, to understand and know the Lord, and to do justice and righteousness in the midst of the earth” (Brenton, modernized). 4QSam-a is reported to contain part of this addition. This needs scholarly review.
The Septuagint begins the verse, “And she left him there before the Lord, and departed to Armathaim” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “sons of Belial,” that is, worthless or wicked men.
Or “the priests’ custom with the people.” Hebrew mishpat, “judgment, right, custom.” Compare the priests’ legal portion in Leviticus 7:31–34 and Deuteronomy 18:3.
The linen ephod here is a simple priestly garment worn by those serving at the sanctuary (compare 22:18; 2 Samuel 6:14), not the high priest’s ornate ephod of Exodus 28.

So 4QSam-a (as reported) and the Septuagint (Brenton, “in return for the loan which you have lent to the Lord,” modernized). The traditional Hebrew text reads “in place of the request which he asked of Yahweh.” Again the verb plays on the name Saul (see 1:20).
The Septuagint lacks this clause about the women at the entrance (Brenton), and 4QSam-a is reported to lack it as well. Compare Exodus 38:8.
Or “the judges” (Hebrew ’elohim). God, or those acting for him, can settle a dispute between people.
The Septuagint reads “when they were servants in Egypt to the house of Pharaoh” (Brenton, modernized), and 4QSam-a is reported to have “servants.”
Hebrew uncertain; literally “kick at” (compare Deuteronomy 32:15). The Septuagint reads “look upon … with a shameless eye” (Brenton, modernized).
The arm is a symbol of strength and vigor.
Hebrew uncertain; literally “you will see an adversary of the dwelling in all that he does good to Israel.” The Septuagint lacks this line (Brenton).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “his eyes … his soul” (Brenton), and 4QSam-a is reported to agree.
So the traditional Hebrew text, “will die as men.” The Septuagint reads “will fall by the sword of men” (Brenton), and 4QSam-a is reported to agree.
Hebrew ’agorah, a small coin or weight of silver, probably a fraction of a shekel (11.5 grams). The exact value is unknown.

verses.text: The boy Samuel was serving Yahweh under Eli. In those days the word of Yahweh was rare; visions did not come often.{a}
One night Eli, whose eyesight had begun to dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his usual place.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out,{b} and Samuel was lying down in the temple of Yahweh, where the ark of God was.
Then Yahweh called Samuel,{c} and he answered, “Here I am!”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” Eli said, “I did not call. Lie down again.” And he went and lay down.
Yahweh called yet again, “Samuel!” Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you called me.” Eli answered, “I did not call, my son. Lie down again.”
Samuel did not yet know Yahweh: the word of Yahweh had not yet been revealed to him.
Yahweh called Samuel a third time. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am; you called me.” Then Eli understood that Yahweh was calling the boy.
So Eli said to Samuel, “Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, ‘Speak, Yahweh, for your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
Yahweh came and stood there, and called as he had the other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel said, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Watch: I am about to do a thing in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears of it ring.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end.
I have told him that I am going to judge his house for all time, for the iniquity that he knew of: his sons were bringing a curse on themselves,{d} and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the guilt of Eli’s house will never be wiped away by sacrifice or offering.”
Samuel lay there until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of Yahweh. But Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Then Eli called Samuel and said, “Samuel, my son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
Eli asked, “What was the word he spoke to you? Do not hide it from me. May God deal with you severely, and more so, if you hide from me anything of all that he told you.”
So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Then Eli said, “He is Yahweh. Let him do what seems good to him.”
Samuel grew up, and Yahweh was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.{e}
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba{f} recognized that Samuel had been confirmed as a prophet of Yahweh.
Yahweh continued to appear at Shiloh, for at Shiloh Yahweh revealed himself to Samuel through the word of Yahweh.{g}

notes.text: Literally “vision was not breaking through.” The Septuagint reads “there was no distinct vision” (Brenton).
That is, it was still night, before dawn. The lampstand in the sanctuary burned from evening until morning (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:2–3).
The Septuagint reads “called Samuel, Samuel” (Brenton has “called, Samuel, Samuel”), and some ancient witnesses agree; compare verse 10.

So the traditional Hebrew text, “were cursing themselves” (or “were treating it lightly”). The Septuagint reads “his sons spoke evil against God” (Brenton). Jewish tradition lists this verse among the places where scribes altered “God” to avoid writing a curse against him, and many scholars think “cursing God” is original.
That is, everything Samuel said came true.
Dan in the far north and Beersheba in the south; the phrase means the whole land.

The Septuagint adds, “and Samuel was trusted by all Israel as a prophet of the Lord from one end of the land to the other; and Eli was very old, and his sons kept going on in wickedness, and their way was evil before the Lord” (Brenton, modernized). Some of this may belong with 4:1.

verses.text: And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle.{a} They pitched camp beside Ebenezer,{b} while the Philistines pitched camp in Aphek.
The Philistines arrayed themselves against Israel, and when the battle spread out, Israel was struck down before the Philistines, and about four thousand men were killed in the ranks in the field.

When the troops returned to the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has Yahweh let us be beaten today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of Yahweh’s covenant here from Shiloh, so that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies.”

So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of Yahweh of Armies, who is enthroned on the cherubim.{c} And Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of Yahweh’s covenant came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great shout, so that the earth rang.
Hearing the noise of the shouting, the Philistines said, “What is this great shouting in the Hebrews’ camp?” When they learned that the ark of Yahweh had come into the camp,
the Philistines were frightened. They said, “God has come into the camp.”{d} And they said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will rescue us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.{e}
Be strong and act like men, Philistines, or you will become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been slaves to you. Be men, and fight!”
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great: thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was taken, and both sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A Benjamite ran from the battle ranks and reached Shiloh that same day, his clothes torn and earth on his head.{f}
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat beside the road, watching,{g} for his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man came into the town to tell the news, the whole town cried out.
Hearing the sound of the outcry, Eli asked, “What is this uproar?” The man hurried over and told Eli.
Eli was ninety-eight years old,{h} and his eyes were fixed so that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, “I have come from the battle; I fled from the ranks today.” Eli asked, “How did things go, my son?”

The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the troops. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been taken.”
At the mention of the ark of God, Eli toppled backward off his seat beside the gate, broke his neck, and died, for he was an old man and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.{i}

Now the wife of Phinehas, his daughter-in-law, was with child and close to delivery. Hearing the report that the ark of God was taken and that her father-in-law and husband were dead, she bent down and gave birth, for her pains came upon her suddenly.
As she was dying, the women attending her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.” But she did not answer or pay attention.
She named the boy Ichabod,{j} saying, “The glory has gone into exile from Israel,” because of the capture of the ark of God and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, “The glory has gone into exile from Israel, for the ark of God has been taken.”

notes.text: The Septuagint begins, “And it came to pass in those days that the Philistines gathered themselves together against Israel to war, and Israel went out to meet them” (Brenton, modernized).
Ebenezer means “stone of help.” The place receives this name in 7:12; the narrator uses the name known to his readers.
The cherubim were winged figures above the cover of the ark (Exodus 25:18–22), pictured as the throne of the invisible God.
Or “gods have come into the camp.” The Septuagint reads “These are the gods that have come to them into the camp” (Brenton, modernized).

Or “with every kind of plague and in the wilderness.” The Philistines’ version of the exodus story is confused, which may be intended. The Septuagint reads “with every plague, and in the wilderness” (Brenton).
Torn clothes and earth on the head were signs of mourning and disaster.
So the traditional reading. The written Hebrew (ketiv) is unclear; the Septuagint reads “upon the seat by the gate looking along the way” (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “ninety years old” (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “twenty years” (Brenton).
Ichabod is usually understood as “Where is the glory?” or “No glory.” The Septuagint has a different form, “Uaibarchaboth” (Brenton, “Uæbarchaboth”), perhaps meaning “Woe for the glory.”

verses.text: After the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.{a}
The Philistines took the ark of God, carried it into the temple of Dagon,{b} and set it up beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next day, there was Dagon, fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of Yahweh. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.

But when they got up early the following morning, there was Dagon again, fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of Yahweh. Dagon’s head and both his hands lay broken off on the threshold; only his trunk{c} was left.
That is why, to this day, neither the priests of Dagon nor anyone who enters Dagon’s temple steps on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod.
Yahweh’s hand weighed heavily on the people of Ashdod. He devastated them and struck them with tumors,{d} both Ashdod and its territory.
When the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand is hard on us and on Dagon our god.”

So they sent for all the rulers of the Philistines,{e} gathered them, and asked, “What should we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” They answered, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved on to Gath.” So they moved the ark of the God of Israel there.
But after they had moved it, Yahweh’s hand was against that city, causing a very great panic. He struck the people of the city, from the least to the greatest, and tumors broke out on them.
Then they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But when the ark of God came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel around to us to kill us and our people!”

They sent and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Send off the ark of the God of Israel and let it return to where it belongs, or it will kill us and our people.” For deadly panic had gripped the whole city; God’s hand was very heavy there.
And the men who did not die were struck with the tumors, and the cry of the city rose up to the heavens.

notes.text: Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron (verses 8–10), with Gaza and Ashkelon, were the five chief cities of the Philistines (6:17). The Septuagint calls them Azotus, Geth, Accaron, Gaza, and Ascalon (Brenton); at verse 10 it reads “Ascalon” instead of Ekron.
Dagon was a West Semitic grain god worshiped by the Philistines (Judges 16:23). The name is probably related to dagan, “grain,” though it was once linked with dag, “fish.”
So the Septuagint, “stump” or “trunk” (Brenton, “stump”). The traditional Hebrew text reads “only Dagon was left on him.”

Hebrew ’ophalim, probably swellings or boils (perhaps the buboes of bubonic plague); the traditional reading (qere) is teḥorim, a word of similar meaning. The Septuagint adds that the hand of the Lord “brought evil upon them, and it burst out upon them into the ships, and mice sprang up in the midst of their country, and there was a great and indiscriminate death in the city” (Brenton, modernized). Compare the gold mice in 6:4–5.
Hebrew seren, a title used only of the Philistine rulers, perhaps related to the Greek word tyrannos, “ruler.”

verses.text: The ark of Yahweh had been in Philistine territory for seven months.{a}
Then the Philistines called in the priests and the diviners and asked, “What should we do with the ark of Yahweh? Tell us how we should send it back to its place.”

They replied, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but by all means pay him back with a guilt offering.{b} Then you will be healed, and you will learn why his hand has not turned away from you.”

They asked, “What guilt offering should we return to him?” They answered, “Five gold tumors and five gold mice, one for each of the rulers of the Philistines, for the same plague struck all of you and your rulers.
So make models of your tumors and models of the mice that are ravaging the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand on you, on your gods, and on your land.
Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt harshly with them, did they not let the people go, and they departed?
So now prepare a new cart, and take two milk cows that have never borne a yoke. Harness the cows to the cart, and bring their calves home behind them.
Take the ark of Yahweh and set it on the cart, and put the gold objects you are paying him as a guilt offering in a chest at its side. Then send it away and let it go.

And watch: if it goes up by the road to its own territory, toward Beth-shemesh,{c} then it is he who has brought this great disaster on us. But if not, we will know that it was not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by chance.”
The men did so. They took two cows that had calved and hitched them to the cart, and shut their calves up at home.
They put the ark of Yahweh on the cart, together with the box holding the gold mice and the models of their tumors.

The cows took the straight way along the road to Beth-shemesh. They went on the one highway, lowing as they walked, turning neither right nor left, while the rulers of the Philistines walked behind them up to the edge of Beth-shemesh.
Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping the wheat harvest in the valley.{d} They raised their eyes and saw the ark, and they rejoiced to see it.
The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A large stone was there. They split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to Yahweh.

The Levites took down the ark of Yahweh and the box beside it with the gold objects, and placed them on the large stone. That day the people of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices to Yahweh.
When the five rulers of the Philistines had seen this, they returned to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold tumors which the Philistines paid back to Yahweh as a guilt offering: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron.

And the gold mice matched the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers, both fortified towns and unwalled villages. The large stone{e} on which they set the ark of Yahweh is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

But Yahweh struck down some of the men of Beth-shemesh because they looked into the ark of Yahweh. He struck down seventy men{f} of the people. And the people mourned because Yahweh had struck the people with a great slaughter.
The men of Beth-shemesh said, “Who can stand before Yahweh, this holy God? And to whom will he go up from us?”
So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim{g} to say, “The Philistines have returned the ark of Yahweh. Come down and take it up to your town.”

notes.text: The Septuagint adds, “and their land brought forth swarms of mice” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew ’asham, the offering that makes amends for a wrong done (Leviticus 5:14–6:7).
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” It lay in Israelite territory about 15 miles (24 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.
The wheat harvest came in May–June.

So some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (Brenton, “the great stone”). The traditional Hebrew text reads “Abel,” perhaps “meadow” or “mourning.” The Hebrew words for “stone” and “meadow” differ by one letter.

So some Hebrew manuscripts and Josephus (as reported). Most Hebrew manuscripts read “seventy men, fifty thousand men,” and the Septuagint reads “seventy men, and fifty thousand men” (Brenton). The larger figure, oddly attached without “and” in the Hebrew, is probably a later addition. The Septuagint also begins the verse differently: “And the sons of Jechonias were not pleased with the men of Bethshemesh, because they saw the ark of the Lord” (Brenton, modernized).
Kiriath-jearim means “town of forests.” It lay about 9 miles (15 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.

verses.text: So the men of Kiriath-jearim came and brought up the ark of Yahweh and took it into the house of Abinadab{a} on the hill, and they set apart Eleazar his son to keep watch over the ark of Yahweh.
From the day the ark came to rest at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, twenty years in all, and the whole house of Israel mourned{b} after Yahweh.

Then Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, “If you are returning to Yahweh with all your heart, then get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths{c} among you. Set your hearts on Yahweh and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the power of the Philistines.”
So the Israelites removed the Baals{d} and the Ashtoreths and served Yahweh alone.
Then Samuel said, “Bring all Israel together at Mizpah,{e} and I will pray to Yahweh for you.”
So they gathered at Mizpah, drew water and poured it out before Yahweh, and fasted that day. There they said, “We have sinned against Yahweh.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, the rulers of the Philistines went up against Israel. Hearing of it, the Israelites were afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to Yahweh our God for us, so that he will save us from the hand of the Philistines.”
So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it whole as a burnt offering to Yahweh. Samuel cried out to Yahweh for Israel, and Yahweh answered him.

As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But Yahweh thundered with a great voice that day against the Philistines and threw them into a panic, and they were struck down before Israel.
The men of Israel went out from Mizpah and chased the Philistines, striking them down as far as a point below Beth-car.{f}
Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen,{g} and he called its name Ebenezer,{h} saying, “Up to this point Yahweh has helped us.”
So the Philistines were humbled and did not again come into Israel’s territory. The hand of Yahweh was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel freed their territory from the Philistines’ control. There was also peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
Year by year he went on a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel at all these places.
Then he would return to Ramah, because his house was there, and there too he judged Israel. And he built an altar there to Yahweh.

notes.text: Abinadab means “my father is generous” or “my father is noble.” Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Or “longed”; the Hebrew verb is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “all the house of Israel looked after the Lord” (Brenton).
Ashtoreth (plural Ashtaroth) was a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war, called Astarte by the Greeks. The Hebrew vowels may imitate boshet, “shame.”
Baal, “lord” or “owner,” was the Canaanite storm god; the plural refers to his local forms and images.
Mizpah means “watchtower.” This Mizpah was in Benjamin, about 8 miles (13 kilometers) north of Jerusalem.
Beth-car means “house of the lamb” or “house of pasture” (uncertain); the site is unknown.
Shen means “tooth,” perhaps a rocky crag. The Septuagint reads “the old city” (Brenton), which suggests the Hebrew name Jeshanah (2 Chronicles 13:19).
Ebenezer means “stone of help.”

verses.text: When Samuel had become old, he made his sons judges over Israel.
His firstborn son was named Joel,{a} and his second, Abijah;{b} they judged at Beersheba.
His sons, however, did not walk in his ways but leaned toward gain; they took bribes and bent justice.
So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, “Look, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us, like all the nations.”
But the request displeased Samuel when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” So Samuel prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to the people in all that they say to you. It is not you they have rejected; they have rejected me from being king over them.
Just as they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until today, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you.
Now then, listen to them; but warn them solemnly, and tell them the practice{c} of the king who will reign over them.”
So Samuel told all the words of Yahweh to the people who had asked him for a king.
He said, “This will be the king’s way with you, the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and put them on his chariots and among his horsemen, and they will run before his chariots.
He will set some as officers over thousands and officers over fifties, and some to plow his plowland and reap his harvest and make his weapons and the fittings of his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.
Your best fields, vineyards, and olive groves he will take and give to his officials.
Of your seed and your vineyards he will take a tenth, and give it to his court officers{d} and his officials.
He will take your male and female slaves, the finest of your young men,{e} and your donkeys, and put them to work for himself.
Of your flocks he will take a tenth, and you yourselves will be his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you have chosen for yourselves, but Yahweh will not answer you on that day.”
But the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “There must be a king over us.
Then we too will be like all the nations, and our king will judge us and go out before us and fight our battles.”
When Samuel had heard all the people’s words, he repeated them in Yahweh’s hearing.
Yahweh said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and make them a king.” So Samuel told the men of Israel, “Go, every man to his own town.”

notes.text: Joel means “Yahweh is God.”
Abijah means “my father is Yahweh.” The Septuagint calls him “Abia” (Brenton).
Hebrew mishpat, “judgment, right, custom”; here the king’s way of doing things, his claims on the people. Compare Deuteronomy 17:14–20.
Hebrew saris, often “eunuch,” but also used more broadly of a court official.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “your good herds” (Brenton), which may reflect a Hebrew word for “cattle” differing by one letter.

verses.text: There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish,{a} son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a man of wealth and standing.{b}
He had a son named Saul,{c} a fine young man; none of the Israelites was finer than he. From his shoulders up he stood taller than all the people.
Now the she-donkeys belonging to Kish the father of Saul had wandered off. Kish told Saul his son, “Take along with you one of the young men, and arise, go and search for the donkeys.”

He passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Shalishah,{d} but they did not find them. Then they passed through the land of Shaalim, and they were not there. Then he passed through the land of Benjamin, and they did not find them.
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul told the young man with him, “Come, we should go back, lest my father leave off caring about the donkeys and become anxious over us.”

But the servant said to him, “Listen, there is a man of God in this town, and the man is held in honor; everything he says surely comes about. Let us go there now. Perhaps he can tell us about the journey we have set out on.”
Saul said to his young man, “Suppose we go; what shall we take to the man? The bread is used up from our sacks, and we have no present to bring the man of God. What is there with us?”
The servant answered Saul again, “Look, I have here in my hand a quarter of a silver coin, about a tenth of an ounce.{e} I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.”
(In former times in Israel, when someone went to ask counsel of God, he would say, “Come, let us go to the seer,” for the one who is now called a prophet{f} used to be called a seer.)
Saul said to his servant, “Well spoken. Come, let us go.” So they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they climbed the ascent to the town, they came upon girls going out to draw water, and they said to them, “Is the seer here?”
They answered, “He is. Look, he is ahead of you. Hurry now, for he has come to town today, because the people have a sacrifice today at the high place.{g}

The moment you go into the town you will find him, before he climbs to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, for he blesses the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited eat. So go up now, for you will find him at once.”
So they went up to the town. Just as they were coming into the middle of the town, Samuel came out facing them, going up to the high place.
Now one day before Saul came, Yahweh had revealed this to Samuel:{h}

“About this time tomorrow I will send to you a man out of Benjamin’s land, and you shall anoint him as leader{i} over my people Israel. He will save my people from the hand of the Philistines, for I have looked upon my people,{j} because their cry has come to me.”
When Samuel saw Saul, Yahweh told him, “Here is the man I spoke to you about. He is the one who will hold my people in check.”{k}
Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and said, “Tell me, please, where is the seer’s house?”
Samuel answered Saul, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for you will eat with me today. In the morning I will let you go, and I will tell you all that is on your mind.

As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not trouble yourself about them, for they have been found. And to whom does all Israel’s desire turn, if not to you and to all your father’s house?”
Saul answered, “Am I not a Benjamite, from the smallest of the tribes of Israel? And is not my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then do you say such a thing to me?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant, led them into the hall, and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, about thirty men.{l}
Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you, the one I told you to set aside.”

So the cook lifted up the thigh and what was on it{m} and set it before Saul. Samuel said, “Here is what was kept back. Set it before you and eat, for it has been kept for you for this appointed time, ever since I said, ‘I have invited the people.’”{n} So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
After they came down from the high place into the town, he talked with Saul on the roof.{o}
They rose early, and at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get up, and I will send you on your way.” Saul got up, and the two of them, he and Samuel, went outside.

When they had come down to the far end of the town, Samuel told Saul, “Tell the young man to pass on before us,” and he passed on. “But as for you, stand here a while, so that I may let you hear the word of God.”

notes.text: Kish probably means “gift” or “bow” (uncertain). The Septuagint spells the names in this genealogy differently (Brenton: Kis, Abiel, Jared, Bachir, Aphec).
Or “a mighty man of valor.” Hebrew gibbor ḥayil can refer to wealth, strength, or social standing.
Saul (Hebrew Shaʾul) means “asked for” (see 1:20 and 8:10).
The locations of Shalishah, Shaalim, and Zuph (verse 5) are uncertain.
Hebrew “a quarter of a shekel of silver,” about 3 grams. Coins were not yet in use; the silver would have been weighed.
Hebrew naviʾ. Seer is Hebrew roʾeh, “one who sees.”
Hebrew bamah, an elevated place of worship, often on a hill.
Literally “had uncovered Samuel’s ear.”
Hebrew nagid, “leader” or “prince,” a title for one designated by God to rule, used here instead of “king.”
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “I have looked upon the humiliation of my people” (Brenton); compare Exodus 3:7.
Or “will rule.” The Hebrew verb usually means “restrain.”
The Septuagint reads “about seventy men” (Brenton).
Or “the thigh and the fat tail.” The Hebrew is uncertain.

Hebrew uncertain; literally “for at the appointed time it was kept for you, saying, ‘I have invited the people.’” The Septuagint reads, “for it is set before you as a testimony in preference to the others; take of it” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads, “and they prepared a lodging for Saul on the roof, and he lay down” (Brenton). Roofs were flat and used as living space.

verses.text: Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on Saul’s head and kissed him and said, “Has not Yahweh anointed you leader over his inheritance?{a}

When you depart from me today, you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb on the border of Benjamin, at Zelzah.{b} They will tell you, ‘The donkeys you set out to seek are found. Now your father has dropped the matter of the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, “What shall I do about my son?”’

Then you will go on from there and come to the oak{c} of Tabor. There three men will meet you on their way up to God at Bethel: one carries three kids, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you are to accept from their hand.

After that you will come to Gibeath-elohim,{d} the place of the Philistine garrison.{e} When you arrive there at the town, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, with lute, hand drum, pipe, and harp going before them, while they prophesy.
Then the Spirit of Yahweh will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into another man.
When these signs have come upon you, do what the occasion calls for, for God is with you.
Then go down ahead of me to Gilgal.{f} I will surely come down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”
As Saul turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart, and all these signs came about that day.
When they came there to the hill, a band of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.
When all who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, the people said to one another, “What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
A man from there answered, “And who is their father?”{g} So it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” He said, “To look for the donkeys. When we saw they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel.”
Saul’s uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul told his uncle, “He let us know for certain that the donkeys were found.” But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he told him nothing.
Then Samuel called the people together to Yahweh at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and distresses. And you have said,{h} ‘No! Set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before Yahweh by your tribes and by your thousands.”{i}
Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot.
He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its families, and the family of the Matrites was taken; and Saul son of Kish was taken.{j} But when they looked for him, he could not be found.
So they inquired again of Yahweh, “Has the man come here yet?”{k} And Yahweh said, “There he is, hidden among the baggage.”
They ran and brought him from there. When he stood among the people, he was taller than any of them from his shoulders up.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one whom Yahweh has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”
Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship,{l} wrote them in a scroll, and laid it up before Yahweh. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to his home.
Saul also went home to Gibeah, and with him went the warriors{m} whose hearts God had touched.

But some worthless men{n} said, “How can this man save us?” They despised him and brought him no gift. But he kept silent.{o} [Nahash king of the Ammonites had been crushing the Gadites and the Reubenites with great cruelty, putting out the right eye of every one of them and letting no one rescue Israel. Among the Israelites east of the Jordan no man remained whose right eye Nahash king of the Ammonites had not put out, except seven thousand men who escaped from the Ammonites and made their way into Jabesh-gilead.]{p}

notes.text: The Septuagint has a longer text: “Has not the Lord anointed you as ruler over his people, over Israel? And you will rule among the people of the Lord and save them out of the hand of their enemies; and this will be the sign to you that the Lord has anointed you as ruler over his inheritance” (Brenton, modernized). The traditional Hebrew text has probably lost the middle of the verse by a copying error, the eye of a scribe skipping from one “the Lord has anointed you” to the next.
Zelzah is otherwise unknown; the Septuagint reads differently (Brenton, “exulting greatly”).
Or “great tree” or “terebinth.”
Gibeath-elohim means “the hill of God.” The Septuagint reads “the hill of God” (Brenton).
Or “a garrison commander” or “a pillar.” Hebrew netsib; the Septuagint takes it as a name, “Nasib the Philistine” (Brenton).
Gilgal means “circle” (of stones), near Jericho (Joshua 4:19–20).
That is, prophets do not inherit their calling; anyone may receive the Spirit. The Septuagint reads “And who is his father?” (Brenton).
So many Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (Brenton, “Nay”). The traditional Hebrew text reads “you said to him,” using a word that sounds the same as “no.”
Or “by your clans.” The Hebrew word ’eleph, “thousand,” can also mean a clan or military unit.
The Septuagint adds, “and they brought near the family of Matri, man by man” (Brenton has “they bring near the family of Mattari, man by man”), a step that appears to have dropped out of the Hebrew.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Will the man come here?” (Brenton).
Or “the custom of the kingdom.” Hebrew mishpat hammelukah; compare 8:9–11 and Deuteronomy 17:14–20.
Hebrew “the force” or “the valiant men”; the Septuagint reads “sons of strength,” that is, warriors (Brenton has “mighty men”).
Hebrew “sons of Belial.”

So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “and he was like one keeping silent.” With a slight change in the Hebrew letters, 4QSam-a and the Septuagint read instead “And about a month later” (Brenton, at the start of 11:1, “And it came to pass about a month after this”), which leads into chapter 11.

The bracketed paragraph is found in 4QSam-a, a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel from Qumran (first century BC), between 10:27 and 11:1. It is not in the traditional Hebrew text or the Septuagint, but Josephus (Jewish Antiquities, book 6) retells the same events, which suggests that he knew a text that had it. Many scholars think the traditional Hebrew text lost the paragraph by a copying error; others think it was added to explain Nahash’s demand in 11:2. The wording here is this translation’s own rendering of the reported text; the scroll is damaged in places. This needs scholarly review.

verses.text: Then Nahash{a} the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead.{b} All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
But Nahash the Ammonite told them, “On this term I will cut a covenant with you, that I put out every right eye of yours, and so lay disgrace on all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Hold off from us for seven days, and we will send messengers into every border of Israel. Then, if no one comes to save us, we will come out to you.”
When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and told these things in the people’s hearing, all the people lifted up their voices and wept.
Now Saul was just then coming from the field after the oxen. Saul said, “Why are the people weeping?” And they related to him the words of the men of Jabesh.
When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and his anger burned hot.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them in pieces, and sent the pieces by messengers throughout the territory of Israel, saying, “Whoever does not come out after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!” Then the dread of Yahweh fell on the people, and they came out as one man.
Saul mustered them at Bezek: there were three hundred thousand men of Israel and thirty thousand men of Judah.{c}

They told the messengers who had come, “Say this to the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will have rescue.’” When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad.
Then the men of Jabesh said to the Ammonites, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may deal with us however you please.”

The next day Saul arranged the people in three companies. They broke into the middle of the camp during the morning watch{d} and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. Those who were left were so scattered that not two of them were left together.
Then the people said to Samuel, “Who was it that said, ‘Shall Saul reign over us?’ Hand the men over, and we will put them to death.”
But Saul said, “No one will be put to death this day, for today Yahweh has brought rescue to Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingship.”

So all the people went to Gilgal, and there at Gilgal they made Saul king before Yahweh.{e} There they offered peace offerings before Yahweh, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.

notes.text: Nahash means “serpent.” On the paragraph that some ancient witnesses place before this verse, see the note at 10:27. In the Septuagint and 4QSam-a (as reported), the verse begins “And about a month later” (Brenton, “And it came to pass about a month after this”).
Jabesh-gilead was a town east of the Jordan, in Gilead; Jabesh means “dry.” Compare Judges 21:8–14.
The Septuagint reads “six hundred thousand” and “seventy thousand” (Brenton). The Hebrew word ’eleph, “thousand,” may also mean a military unit, which would make the figures much smaller.
Hebrew “in the morning watch,” the last of the three watches of the night, from about 2 a.m. until about 6 a.m.
The Septuagint reads “and Samuel anointed Saul there to be king before the Lord” (Brenton), and it ends the verse, “and Samuel and all Israel rejoiced greatly” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: Samuel said to all Israel, “I have listened to your voice in all that you said to me, and I have set a king over you.
Now look, the king walks before you. As for me, I am old and gray-headed, and my sons, look, they are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.

Here I am. Testify against me before Yahweh and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken, or whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I crushed? From whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it?{a} Tell me, and I will repay you.”
They said, “You have not defrauded us or crushed us, nor taken anything at all from anyone’s hand.”
He said to them, “Yahweh is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand.” And they said,{b} “He is witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “Yahweh is witness,{c} who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up from the land of Egypt.
So now take your stand, so that I may plead with you before Yahweh about all the righteous acts of Yahweh which he did for you and for your fathers.
When Jacob went into Egypt,{d} and your fathers cried out to Yahweh, Yahweh sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place.

But they forgot Yahweh their God, so he sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor,{e} and into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the king of Moab, and these fought against them.
Then they cried out to Yahweh and said, ‘We have sinned, for we have forsaken Yahweh and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. But now rescue us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.’
And Yahweh sent Jerubbaal,{f} Bedan,{g} Jephthah, and Samuel,{h} and rescued you from the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in security.
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, ‘No, a king shall reign over us,’ though Yahweh your God was your king.
Now look, here is the king whom you chose, for whom you asked. See, Yahweh has set a king over you.
If you will fear Yahweh and serve him and listen to his voice and not rebel against Yahweh’s command, and if both you and the king who reigns over you follow Yahweh your God, all will be well.{i}
But if you will not listen to Yahweh’s voice, but rebel against Yahweh’s command, then the hand of Yahweh will be against you, as it was against your fathers.{j}
Now therefore take your stand and see this great thing that Yahweh will do before your eyes.

Is it not wheat harvest today?{k} I will call on Yahweh, and he will send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see that the wrong you have done in Yahweh’s sight is great, in asking for yourselves a king.”
So Samuel called on Yahweh, and Yahweh sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared Yahweh and Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray for your servants to Yahweh your God, that we do not die; for we have added to all our sins this evil of asking for ourselves a king.”
Samuel said to the people, “Fear not. You have indeed done all this evil; only, do not turn away from following Yahweh, but serve Yahweh with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after empty things,{l} which neither profit nor rescue, for they are empty.
For Yahweh will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name, because it has pleased Yahweh to make you a people for himself.
As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against Yahweh by ceasing to pray for you. I will instruct you in the good and right way.
Only fear Yahweh and serve him faithfully with all your heart, for consider what great things he has done for you.
But if you keep on doing evil, you will be swept off, you and your king alike.”

notes.text: So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “a bribe, even a sandal? Testify against me” (Brenton, modernized), and Sirach 46:19 is reported to reflect a similar text.
So many Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint. The traditional Hebrew text reads “he said.”
“Is witness” is supplied from the Septuagint (Brenton: “The Lord who appointed Moses and Aaron is witness”); the Hebrew lacks the word.
The Septuagint adds, “and his sons, and Egypt humbled them” (Brenton, modernized).
The Septuagint reads “Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor” (Brenton has “Sisara captain of the host of Jabis king of Asor”).
Jerubbaal is another name for Gideon (Judges 6:32).
So the traditional Hebrew text; Bedan is not named in Judges. The Septuagint reads “Barak” (Brenton, “Barac”), which fits Judges 4–5.
So the traditional Hebrew text. Some ancient witnesses, including the Syriac, are reported to read “Samson.”
“All will be well” is supplied; the Hebrew sentence breaks off after “your God.”
Literally “against you and against your fathers,” as in the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “against you and against your king” (Brenton, “upon you and upon your king”).
The wheat harvest came in May–June, the dry season, when rain was very rare.
Hebrew tohu, “emptiness,” the word used in Genesis 1:2 (“formless”).

verses.text: Saul was [...] years old when he became king, and he reigned [...] two years over Israel.{a}

Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash{b} and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan{c} at Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent away, each to his tent.
Jonathan struck down the Philistine garrison{d} at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Then Saul had the ram’s horn blown throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!”{e}
And all Israel heard the news: “Saul has struck down the Philistine garrison, and Israel has also become a stench to the Philistines.” And the people were called out after Saul to Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight with Israel: thirty thousand chariots,{f} six thousand horsemen, and people as many as the sand on the shore of the sea. They came up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.{g}
When the men of Israel saw that they were in a tight place, for the people were hard pressed, the people hid themselves in caves, in thickets, among the rocks, in cellars,{h} and in cisterns.
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.
He waited seven days, the time set by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people began to scatter from him.
So Saul said, “Bring the burnt offering and the peace offerings here to me.” And he offered the burnt offering.
Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, there was Samuel coming. Saul went out to meet him and to greet him.{i}
Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul said, “When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and you did not come within the days appointed, and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash,
I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of Yahweh.’ So I forced myself and offered the burnt offering.”
Samuel said to Saul, “You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the command of Yahweh your God which he commanded you. For now Yahweh would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.

But now your kingdom will not last. Yahweh has sought out for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him leader over his people, because you have not kept what Yahweh commanded you.”
Then Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin.{j} Saul counted the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and Jonathan his son, and the people found with them, stayed in Geba of Benjamin, and the Philistines were encamped in Michmash.
Raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies. One company turned toward the road to Ophrah, to the land of Shual;
another company turned toward the road to Beth-horon; and another company turned toward the border road that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim,{k} toward the wilderness.
Now no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel, for the Philistines had said, “Otherwise the Hebrews will make themselves swords or spears.”
So all Israel had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen each man his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, and his sickle.{l}
The charge was about a quarter of an ounce of silver{m} for the plowshares and the mattocks, and about an eighth of an ounce{n} for the forks and the axes and for setting the goads.
So it was on the day of battle that neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan; but with Saul and with Jonathan his son they were found.
And the Philistine garrison went out to the pass of Michmash.

notes.text: The Hebrew text of this verse is incomplete. It reads literally, “Saul was a year old when he became king, and he reigned two years over Israel.” A number has evidently been lost before “year,” and probably before “two years” as well. The verse is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton). Acts 13:21 gives Saul’s reign as forty years, and Josephus is reported to give twenty or forty years in different passages; some later Greek manuscripts are reported to read “thirty years old.” The bracketed gaps mark the missing numbers. This needs scholarly review.
Michmash was a town about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem.
Jonathan means “Yahweh has given.”
Or “the garrison commander” or “the Philistine pillar.” Hebrew netsib; the Septuagint reads “Nasib the Philistine” (Brenton). Likewise in verse 4.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “The slaves have revolted” (Brenton, “The servants have despised us”), taking the Hebrew letters differently.
So the traditional Hebrew text and the Septuagint (Brenton). Some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac are reported to read “three thousand,” which may be original.
Beth-aven means “house of wickedness,” possibly a mocking name for Bethel (“house of God”); compare Hosea 4:15.
Or “in tombs” or “in strongholds.” The Hebrew word is rare.
Literally “to bless him.”

So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint has a longer text: “and departed from Gilgal, and the rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the men of war, when they had come out of Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin” (Brenton, modernized and slightly simplified). The Hebrew may have lost words by a copying error.
Zeboim means “hyenas.”
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “sickle”). The Hebrew repeats the word for “plowshare.”

Hebrew pim, a weight found in excavations, about two-thirds of a shekel, about 8 grams. The meaning of this verse was unknown until such weights were found; the Septuagint reads “three shekels” (Brenton).
Hebrew “a third of a shekel,” about 4 grams.

verses.text: One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us go across to the Philistine outpost over on that side.” But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying at the outskirts of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron, and the people with him were about six hundred men.
Ahijah{a} son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas son of Eli, the priest of Yahweh at Shiloh, was carrying the ephod.{b} The people did not know that Jonathan had gone.

Between the passes by which Jonathan sought to cross over to the Philistine garrison there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other was Seneh.{c}
The one crag rose on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men. It may be that Yahweh will act for us, for nothing can hinder Yahweh from saving, whether by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer said to him, “Do everything that is in your heart. Turn wherever you wish; here I am with you, heart for heart.”{d}
Then Jonathan said, “Look, we will cross over to the men and let them see us.
If they say to us, ‘Stand still until we reach you,’ then we will stand where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ then we will go up, for Yahweh has given them into our hand. This will be the sign to us.”
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine garrison. The Philistines said, “See, the Hebrews are creeping out of the holes where they hid themselves.”

The men of the garrison called to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us, and we will teach you something!” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Come up after me, for Yahweh has given them into the hand of Israel.”
Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. They fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer finished them off behind him.
That first slaughter which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made was about twenty men, within about half an acre of land.{e}
Terror spread through the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and the raiders also trembled. The earth quaked, and it became a terror from God.{f}
Saul’s lookouts in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and there was the crowd, melting away and running here and there.{g}
Then Saul said to the people who were with him, “Count now and see who has gone from us.” When they had counted, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.
Saul told Ahijah, “Bring near the ark of God.”{h} For the ark of God was with the Israelites at that time.
While Saul was talking to the priest, the uproar in the camp of the Philistines kept growing louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Then Saul and all the people with him were called together, and they went into the battle. And there was every man’s sword against his fellow, in very great confusion.
The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, who had gone up with them into the camp, also turned{i} to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
Likewise all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, and they too pursued hard after them in the battle.
So Yahweh saved Israel that day, and the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.{j}

The men of Israel were hard pressed that day, for Saul had bound the people under an oath, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening, until I have taken vengeance on my enemies.”{k} So none of the people tasted food.
All the people{l} came into the forest, and there was honey on the ground.
When the people entered the forest, there was the honey dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard when his father bound the people with the oath. So he reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.{m}
Then one of the people said, “Your father strictly bound the people with an oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’” And the people were faint.
Jonathan said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better if the people had eaten freely today from the plunder of their enemies which they found! For now the slaughter among the Philistines has not been great.”
They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint.
The people rushed greedily on the plunder. They took sheep and cattle and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate them with the blood.
Then they told Saul, “Look, the people are sinning against Yahweh by eating with the blood.” He said, “You have dealt faithlessly. Roll a large stone to me here today.”{n}

Saul said, “Scatter among the people and say to them, ‘Bring to me each man his ox and each his sheep; slaughter them on this stone and eat, and do not sin against Yahweh by eating with the blood.’” That night all the people brought each his ox in his hand and slaughtered it there.
And Saul built an altar to Yahweh; it was the first altar he built to Yahweh.

Then Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them.” They said, “Do whatever seems good in your eyes.” Then the priest said, “Let us come near to God over here.”
So Saul asked counsel of God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?” But he did not answer him that day.
Saul said, “Draw near here, all the leaders{o} of the people; learn and see in what way this sin has happened today.
For as Yahweh lives, who saves Israel, even if it lies in my son Jonathan, he shall surely die.” But not one of all the people answered him.
Then he said to all Israel, “You be on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will be on the other side.” The people said to Saul, “Do what seems good to you.”
Therefore Saul said to Yahweh, the God of Israel, “Give Thummim.”{p} And Jonathan and Saul were taken by lot, and the people went free.
Saul said, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son.” And Jonathan was taken.{q}
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, “I did indeed taste a little honey with the end of the rod in my hand. Here I am; I must die.”
Saul said, “May God do so, and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan.”

But the people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great deliverance in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day.” So the people ransomed Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.

When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he made war all around against all his enemies: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he inflicted punishment.{r}
He acted valiantly and struck down the Amalekites, and rescued Israel from the hand of those who plundered them.
Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi,{s} and Malchi-shua.{t} The names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger was Michal.{u}
The name of Saul’s wife was Ahinoam,{v} daughter of Ahimaaz. His army’s commander was named Abner,{w} son of Ner, Saul’s uncle.
Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.
There was fierce war against the Philistines all the days of Saul. Whenever Saul saw any mighty man or any valiant man, he took him into his service.

notes.text: Ahijah means “brother of Yahweh” or “Yahweh is my brother.”
The ephod here is a priestly garment used in seeking God’s answer (compare 23:9–12).
Bozez perhaps means “shining” and Seneh “thorny” (both uncertain).
So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “Turn; here I am with you as your heart.” The Septuagint reads “my heart is as your heart” (Brenton, modernized).

Hebrew “in about half a furrow of a yoke of field,” probably half the area that a pair of oxen could plow in a day. The phrase is obscure; the Septuagint reads differently, “with darts and slings and stones of the field” (Brenton, modernized). This needs scholarly review.
Or “a very great terror.”
So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “and it went and hither.” The Septuagint reads “thrown into confusion on every side” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads, “Bring the ephod, for he wore the ephod at that time before Israel” (Brenton, modernized), which agrees with verse 3 and with verse 19.
So the Septuagint and other ancient witnesses. The Hebrew reads “who had gone up with them into the camp all around, they also.”
The Septuagint adds, “and all the people with Saul were about ten thousand men, and the battle spread to every city in the hill country of Ephraim” (Brenton, modernized and condensed).
The Septuagint begins the verse, “And Saul committed a great error of ignorance in that day” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “all the land.” The Hebrew of verses 25–26 is difficult.
So the ketiv (written text); the qere (traditional reading) is “his eyes saw clearly.”
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Out of Gittaim roll a great stone to me here” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “cornerstones,” a picture of leaders.

So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “Give perfect,” where the Hebrew word may be read as Thummim. The Septuagint has a longer text, reading in Greek “why have you not answered your servant this day? Is the guilt in me or in my son Jonathan? Lord God of Israel, give clear signs; and if the lot should declare this, give to your people Israel, give holiness” (Brenton, modernized). Many scholars think the Greek reflects a Hebrew text that read, “If this guilt is in me or in my son Jonathan, give Urim; but if it is in your people Israel, give Thummim,” and that the traditional text lost words by a copying error. Urim and Thummim were the sacred lots (Exodus 28:30). This needs scholarly review.
The Septuagint adds, “whomever the Lord shall take by lot, let him die. And the people said to Saul, This thing is not to be done. And Saul prevailed against the people” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “he was victorious” (Brenton), from a Hebrew word with similar letters.
The Septuagint reads “Jessiu” (Brenton). Ishvi may be another name for Abinadab (31:2; 1 Chronicles 8:33) or for Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:8). Ishvi perhaps means “man of Yahweh” (uncertain).
Malchi-shua means “my king is salvation” or “king of wealth” (uncertain).
Merab perhaps means “increase”; Michal perhaps means “who is like God?” (both uncertain).
Ahinoam means “my brother is pleasantness.”
Abner means “my father is a lamp.”

verses.text: Samuel said to Saul, “It was I whom Yahweh sent to anoint you king over his people, over Israel. Now therefore listen to the sound of the words of Yahweh.
This is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘I will punish what Amalek did to Israel, how he set himself against him on the way when he came up out of Egypt.{a}
Now go and strike Amalek, and devote to destruction{b} all that he has. Do not spare him, but put to death man and woman, child and nursing infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’”
So Saul summoned the people and mustered them at Telaim:{c} two hundred thousand on foot, and ten thousand from Judah.{d}
Saul came as far as the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the ravine.

Then Saul said to the Kenites, “Go, depart, go down from among the Amalekites, so that I do not destroy you with them, for you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt.” So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
