Then Saul struck the Amalekites, from Havilah until you come to Shur, which faces Egypt.
He took Agag{e} king of the Amalekites alive, and devoted all the people to destruction with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep and of the cattle, the fat animals{f} and the lambs, and all that was good, and were not willing to destroy them. But everything that was despised and worthless, that they destroyed.
Then the word of Yahweh came to Samuel:
“I regret that I made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not carried out my words.” Samuel was angry,{g} and he cried out to Yahweh all night.
Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. Samuel was told, “Saul came to Carmel,{h} and there he set up a monument for himself; then he turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal.”{i}
When Samuel came to Saul, Saul said to him, “Blessed are you by Yahweh! I have carried out the word of Yahweh.”
Samuel said, “Then what is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of cattle that I hear?”
Saul said, “They brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the cattle to sacrifice to Yahweh your God; the rest we have devoted to destruction.”
Then Samuel said to Saul, “Stop! Let me tell you what Yahweh said to me this night.” He said to him, “Speak.”
Samuel said, “Though you were small in your own eyes, were you not made head of the tribes of Israel? Yahweh anointed you king over Israel.
And Yahweh sent you on a journey and said, ‘Go, devote the sinners, the Amalekites, to destruction, and fight against them until they are wiped out.’
Why then did you not obey the voice of Yahweh? Why did you swoop down on the plunder and do what was evil in Yahweh’s sight?”
Saul said to Samuel, “But I did obey the voice of Yahweh. I went on the mission on which Yahweh sent me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I devoted the Amalekites to destruction.
But the people took from the plunder sheep and cattle, the best of what was devoted, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God in Gilgal.”
Samuel said, “Does Yahweh delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to the voice of Yahweh? Look, to obey is better than sacrifice, to pay heed than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance like wickedness and household idols.{j} Because you have rejected the word of Yahweh, he has also rejected you from being king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, for I have transgressed the command of Yahweh and your words, because I feared the people and listened to their voice.
Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me, so that I may bow in worship before Yahweh.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you, for you have rejected the word of Yahweh, and Yahweh has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
As Samuel turned to go away, Saul{k} seized the hem of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, “Yahweh has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you.
Also the Glory{l} of Israel will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man, that he should change his mind.”
Then Saul said, “I have sinned. Yet honor me now, please, before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, so that I may bow in worship before Yahweh your God.”
So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed in worship before Yahweh.
Then Samuel said, “Bring Agag king of the Amalekites here to me.” Agag came to him in fetters.{m} Agag said, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”{n}
Samuel said, “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before Yahweh in Gilgal.
Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house at Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel mourned over Saul. And Yahweh regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

notes.text: See Exodus 17:8–16 and Deuteronomy 25:17–19.
Hebrew ḥerem, the giving over of people and goods to God by total destruction. Likewise throughout this chapter.
Telaim (“lambs”) is perhaps the Telem of Joshua 15:24. The Septuagint reads “Gilgal” (Brenton, “Galgala”).
The Septuagint reads “four hundred thousand” and “thirty thousand” (Brenton). On “thousand,” see the note at 11:8.
Agag is perhaps a royal title of the Amalekite kings (compare Numbers 24:7); its meaning is uncertain.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean “the second-born” or “the fattened.”
Or “was distressed.”
This Carmel is a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Hebron (compare 25:2), not Mount Carmel.
The Septuagint adds that when Samuel came to Gilgal, Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord from the best of the plunder taken from Amalek (Brenton).
Hebrew teraphim. The Hebrew of this line is difficult. The Septuagint reads differently: “idols bring on pain and grief” (Brenton).
So the Septuagint (Brenton) and 4QSam-a (reported). The Hebrew lacks “Saul.”
Or “the Eternal One” or “the Splendor.” Hebrew netsaḥ.
Or “cheerfully” or “haltingly.” The Hebrew word is uncertain; the Septuagint reads “trembling” (Brenton).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads, “Is death thus bitter?” (Brenton); the shorter Greek may reflect a Hebrew text reported to read “Surely death is bitter.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you go on mourning for Saul, when I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse{a} the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears of it, he will kill me.” Yahweh said, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh.’
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will make known to you what you shall do. You shall anoint for me the one whom I name to you.”
Samuel did what Yahweh said and came to Bethlehem.{b} The elders of the town came trembling to meet him and said, “Is your coming peaceable?”{c}
He said, “Peaceable. I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh. Make yourselves holy and come with me to the sacrifice.” He also consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came, he looked at Eliab{d} and thought, “Surely Yahweh’s anointed stands before him.”
But Yahweh told Samuel, “Pay no regard to how he looks or to how tall he stands, because I have rejected him. For it is not as man sees:{e} man looks at the eyes,{f} but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab{g} and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “Neither has Yahweh chosen this one.”
Then Jesse made Shammah{h} pass by. And he said, “Neither has Yahweh chosen this one.”
Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, “Yahweh has not chosen these.”

Then Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all the young men?” He said, “There is still the youngest, but he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and fetch him, for we will not sit down to eat{i} until he comes here.”
So he sent and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a fine appearance. Yahweh said, “Arise, anoint him, for this is he.”
Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of Yahweh rushed upon David{j} from that day forward. Then Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of Yahweh departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh tormented him.{k}
Saul’s servants said to him, “Look now, an evil spirit from God is tormenting you.

Let our lord command your servants who are before you to seek out a man skilled at playing the lyre. Then, when the evil spirit from God is upon you, he will play with his hand, and you will be well.”
So Saul told his servants, “Look out for me a man who can play well, and bring him to me.”

One of the young men answered, “Look, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who is skilled in playing, a valiant man, a man of war, wise in speech, a man of good presence; and Yahweh is with him.”
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me David your son, who is with the sheep.”
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread,{l} a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to Saul by his son David.
So David came to Saul and stood before him. Saul came to love him very much, and he became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent to Jesse, saying, “Let David stand before me, for he has found favor in my eyes.”
And whenever the spirit from God came over Saul, David would take the lyre and play with his hand. Then Saul found relief and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.

notes.text: Jesse perhaps means “Yahweh exists” or “man” (uncertain).
Bethlehem means “house of bread.”
Or “Do you come in peace?” The Septuagint adds “you seer” (Brenton).
Eliab means “my God is father.”
The Hebrew is brief, literally “for not what man sees.” The Septuagint reads “for God sees not as a man looks” (Brenton).
That is, at outward appearance.
Abinadab means “my father is generous.”
Shammah is perhaps a short form of a name meaning “Yahweh has heard” (uncertain). He is called Shimeah in 2 Samuel 13:3 and Shimea in 1 Chronicles 2:13.
So the Septuagint. The Hebrew reads “will not turn around” or “sit around,” probably at the meal.
David perhaps means “beloved” (uncertain). This is the first time David is named.
Or “terrified him.”

Hebrew ḥamor, “donkey,” which can also be read ḥomer, a dry measure of about 6 bushels (220 liters). The Septuagint reads “a homer of bread” (Brenton), but a donkey loaded with bread is the more likely meaning.

verses.text: The Philistines gathered their armies for war. They were gathered at Socoh,{a} which belongs to Judah, and they encamped at Ephes-dammim,{b} between Socoh and Azekah.
Saul and the men of Israel were gathered and camped in the Valley of Elah,{c} and they drew up their battle line to meet the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with the valley between them.
Then a champion{d} came out from the camp of the Philistines, whose name was Goliath,{e} of Gath. His height was about nine feet nine inches.{f}
He had a bronze helmet on his head, and he wore a coat of scale armor; the weight of the coat was about a hundred and twenty-five pounds{g} of bronze.
Bronze greaves were on his legs, and a bronze javelin{h} was slung between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and the head of his spear weighed about fifteen pounds{i} of iron. And the shield-bearer went before him.

He stood up and called out to the lines of Israel, “What is this, coming out to set the battle in order? Am I not the Philistine, and you Saul’s servants? Pick out a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.
If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us.”
And the Philistine said, “I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, and let us fight together.”
When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were shattered and very much afraid.
Now David was the son of that Ephrathite{j} of Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons, and in the days of Saul the man was old, advanced in years.{k}
The three oldest sons of Jesse had gone after Saul to the war. The names of his three sons who went to the war were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul,
but David would go back and forth from Saul to tend his father’s sheep at Bethlehem.
Forty days the Philistine drew near, early and late, and presented himself.
Jesse said to David his son, “Take now for your brothers about three-fifths of a bushel{l} of this roasted grain and these ten loaves, and run with them to the camp to your brothers.
And bring these ten slices of cheese{m} to the commander of their thousand. See how your brothers are faring, and bring back some token from them.{n}
Saul and they and all the men of Israel are in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.”

David rose early in the morning, left the sheep with a keeper, took the provisions, and went as Jesse had commanded him. He came to the encampment{o} just as the army was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up, line facing line.
David left his baggage in the care of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the battle line. He came and asked his brothers how they were.
As he was talking with them, there was the champion, the Philistine of Gath named Goliath, coming up out of the ranks of the Philistines. He spoke the same words as before, and David heard them.
All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were greatly afraid.

The men of Israel said, “Have you seen this man who is coming up? He comes up to defy Israel. The king will make the man who kills him very rich, will give him his daughter, and will make his father’s house free{p} in Israel.”

David asked the men standing near him, “What shall be done for the man who strikes down this Philistine and removes the disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the ranks of the living God?”
The people answered him with the same words: “So it will be done for the man who kills him.”

Eliab his oldest brother heard when he spoke to the men, and Eliab’s anger burned against David. He said, “Why have you come down? With whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart; you came down to watch the battle.”
David said, “What have I done now? Was it not only a word?”
He turned from him toward another and spoke in the same way, and the people gave him the same answer as before.
The words that David spoke were overheard and told before Saul, and he had him brought.{q}
David said to Saul, “Let no one’s heart fail because of him.{r} Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are only a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth.”
But David said to Saul, “Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock,
I went out after it and struck it and rescued the lamb from its mouth. If it rose against me, I seized it by its beard,{s} struck it, and killed it.
Your servant has struck down both lion and bear, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has taunted the ranks of the living God.”{t}
David said, “Yahweh who rescued me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go, and Yahweh be with you.”
Then Saul dressed David in his own garments, set a bronze helmet on his head, and dressed him in a coat of mail.
David strapped his sword over his garments and tried to walk, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, “I cannot walk in these, for I have not tested them.” So David took them off.

He took his staff in his hand and chose for himself five smooth stones from the stream bed and put them into the shepherd’s bag he had, into the pouch. With his sling in his hand, he drew near to the Philistine.
The Philistine came on and drew near to David, with the shield-bearer in front of him.{u}
When the Philistine looked about and saw David, he scorned him, for he was but a lad, ruddy and good to look at.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?”{v} And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and to the beasts of the field.”

Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the ranks of Israel, whom you have defied.

This day Yahweh will shut you up into my hand. I will strike you and take your head from you, and I will give the corpses{w} of the camp of the Philistines this day to the birds of the sky and to the wild animals of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,
and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh does not save by sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”
When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David hurried and ran toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.{x}
David put his hand into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead,{y} and he fell on his face to the ground.
So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck down the Philistine and killed him; there was no sword in David’s hand.{z}
Then David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and of Judah rose up with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai{aa} and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded of the Philistines fell along the road from Shaaraim{ab} as far as Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites came back from their hot pursuit of the Philistines and plundered their camp.
David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem,{ac} but he put his weapons in his tent.
When Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, “Abner, whose son is this youth?” Abner said, “As you live, O king, I do not know.”{ad}
The king said, “Ask whose son the young man is.”
When David returned from killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand.
Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David answered, “The son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.”

notes.text: Socoh means “thorny place.” The Septuagint text of chapters 17–18 is much shorter than the traditional Hebrew text. The oldest complete Greek manuscript (Codex Vaticanus) lacks about two-fifths of the Hebrew material, including 17:12–31, 17:41, 17:48b, 17:50, 17:55–18:5, and other parts of chapter 18. Brenton’s edition prints 17:12–31 (from other Greek manuscripts) but lacks 17:41, 17:50, 17:55–58, 18:1–5, 18:9–11, 18:17–19, and 18:30. Scholars debate whether the shorter Greek text represents an earlier form of the story or a shortening made to remove tensions with chapter 16 (for example, Saul already knows David in 16:21–23 but asks who he is in 17:55–58). This needs scholarly review.
Ephes-dammim means “boundary of blood.”
Elah means “terebinth” or “great tree.”
Hebrew “the man of the between,” that is, one who fights between two armies in single combat. Likewise in verse 23.
The meaning of the name Goliath is uncertain.

Hebrew “six cubits and a span,” about 2.9 meters. 4QSam-a (as reported) and the Septuagint (Brenton) read “four cubits and a span,” about 6 feet 9 inches (2 meters), which Josephus is also reported to support. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), and a span about 9 inches. This needs scholarly review.
Hebrew “5,000 shekels,” about 57 kilograms.
Or “scimitar.”
Hebrew “600 shekels,” about 6.9 kilograms.
Ephrathite means a man from Ephrathah, the district around Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; Micah 5:2). Brenton prints verses 12–31, but the oldest Greek manuscript lacks them (see the note at verse 1).
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “passed for an old man among men”) and the Syriac (reported). The Hebrew reads “came among men.”
Hebrew “an ephah,” about 22 liters.
Literally “ten cuts of milk,” probably cheeses or curds.
Or “and take their pledge,” perhaps a sign that David had delivered the food.
Or “the circle of wagons.”
That is, free from taxes or forced labor.
Verses 12–31 are lacking in the oldest Greek manuscript (see the note at verse 1).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Let not the heart of my lord be cast down within him” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “its jaw.” The Septuagint reads “its throat” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds, “Shall I not go and strike him, and take away a reproach this day from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised one?” (Brenton, modernized).
This verse is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript.
The Septuagint adds, “and stones? And David said, No, but worse than a dog” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “your limbs and the limbs of the army of the Philistines” (Brenton, modernized).
The second half of the verse (“David hurried … the Philistine”) is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds “through the helmet” (Brenton, “the stone penetrated through the helmet into his forehead”).
This verse is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Gath” (Brenton, “Geth”), which fits the end of the verse.
Shaaraim means “two gates.” The Septuagint reads “the gates” (Brenton).
Jerusalem was not yet in Israelite hands (see 2 Samuel 5:6–9). The statement may anticipate a later time.
Verses 55–58 and 18:1–5 are lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript (see the note at verse 1).

verses.text: When he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.{a}
Saul took him that day and would not let him go back to his father’s house.
And Jonathan and David cut a covenant, since he loved him as his own soul.
Jonathan stripped off the robe that was on him and gave it to David, with his garments, even his sword, his bow, and his belt.
David went out wherever Saul sent him and had success,{b} and Saul set him over the men of war. It was good in the eyes of all the people and also in the eyes of Saul’s servants.

As they came in, when David came back from the slaughter of the Philistine, women came out of all the towns of Israel singing and dancing to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with joy, and with three-stringed instruments.{c}
The women sang to one another as they made merry: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and me they have credited with thousands. What more can he have but the kingdom?”{d}
And Saul eyed David from that day on.{e}
The next day an evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved{f} inside his house, while David was playing the lyre with his hand, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand.
And Saul flung the spear, saying to himself, “I will strike David through, into the wall.” But twice David turned aside from before him.
Saul was afraid of David, because Yahweh was with him but had departed from Saul.{g}
So Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander of a thousand. He went out and came in before the people.
David had success in all his ways, and Yahweh was with him.
When Saul saw that he was having great success, he stood in awe of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.

Then Saul told David, “See, Merab my elder daughter: her I will give you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight Yahweh’s battles.” For Saul thought, “Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”{h}
David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my life, or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?”
But at the time when Merab, Saul’s daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel{i} the Meholathite as a wife.
Now Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David. They told Saul, and the matter was right in his eyes.
Saul thought, “I will give her to him, so that she may be a snare to him and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” So Saul said to David a second time, “You shall now be my son-in-law.”{j}
Saul gave orders to his servants: “Talk with David privately and say, ‘See, the king takes pleasure in you, and all his servants love you. So now, be son-in-law to the king.’”
So Saul’s servants spoke those words in David’s ears. And David said, “Does it seem a little thing in your eyes to become the king’s son-in-law, since I am a poor man and lightly esteemed?”
Saul’s servants reported to him, “These are the words David spoke.”

Then Saul said, “This is what you are to tell David: ‘The king has no wish for a bride-price{k} other than a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to take vengeance on the king’s enemies.’” For Saul planned to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
When his servants told David these words, the matter was right in David’s eyes, to become the king’s son-in-law. Before the days had expired,{l}

David arose and went, he and his men, and struck down two hundred men{m} of the Philistines. David brought their foreskins, and they were counted out in full to the king, that he might be the king’s son-in-law. And Saul gave him Michal his daughter as a wife.
Saul saw and knew that Yahweh was with David, and that Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved him.{n}
So Saul was still more afraid of David, and Saul became David’s enemy continually.{o}
Then the princes of the Philistines went out to war; and whenever they went out, David prospered more than all Saul’s servants, so that his name became very dear.{p}

notes.text: Verses 1–5 are lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript (see the note at 17:1).
Or “acted wisely.” The Hebrew verb sakal means both. Likewise in verses 14, 15, and 30.

Hebrew shalishim, perhaps “triangles,” “lutes,” or “three-stringed instruments” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “cymbals” (Brenton). The Septuagint lacks “when David returned from striking down the Philistine” and “to meet King Saul,” and reads “to meet David” (Brenton).
The last sentence is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton).
Verses 9–11 are lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript.
Hebrew “prophesied,” here of uncontrolled, frenzied behavior.
The Septuagint reads only “And Saul was alarmed on account of David” (Brenton).
Verses 17–19 are lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript.
Adriel means “my help is God.” Compare 2 Samuel 21:8, where the traditional Hebrew text names Michal instead of Merab.
The Hebrew phrase translated “a second time” is obscure (literally “by two”). The last sentence is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton).
Hebrew mohar, the price paid by the groom to the bride’s family.
The last clause (“Before the days had expired”) is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “a hundred men” (Brenton), agreeing with verse 25 and with 2 Samuel 3:14.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “and that all Israel loved him” (Brenton).
The last clause is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton).
This verse is lacking in the Septuagint (Brenton) and in the oldest Greek manuscript.

verses.text: Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants about putting David to death. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, delighted greatly in David.
So Jonathan told David, “Saul my father is seeking to put you to death. Now therefore be on your guard in the morning; stay in a hidden place and conceal yourself.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak about you to my father. If I learn anything, I will tell you.”

So Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, “Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have been very good toward you.

For he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine, and Yahweh worked a great deliverance for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then would you sin against innocent blood by putting David to death without cause?”
Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan, and Saul swore, “As Yahweh lives, he shall not be put to death.”
Then Jonathan called David, and Jonathan told him all these things. Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.
War broke out again, and David went out to fight with the Philistines. He struck them down with a great slaughter, and they fled from before him.
Then an evil spirit from Yahweh came upon Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David was playing the lyre with his hand.
Saul sought to strike David into the wall with the spear, but he slipped aside from before Saul, so that the spear struck into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and to kill him in the morning. But Michal, David’s wife, told him, “If you do not save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be put to death.”
So Michal let David down through the window, and he went away, fled, and escaped.
Michal took the household idol{a} and laid it on the bed, put a net of goats’ hair{b} at its head, and covered it with the garment.
When Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, “He is sick.”
Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, “Bring him up to me in the bed, so that I may put him to death.”
When the messengers came in, there was the household idol in the bed, with the net of goats’ hair at its head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me like this and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?” Michal answered Saul, “He said to me, ‘Let me go. Why should I kill you?’”
Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth.{c}
It was told Saul, “Look, David is at Naioth in Ramah.”

Then Saul sent messengers to take David. When they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers, and they also prophesied.
When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.
Then he himself went to Ramah and came to the great cistern that is at Secu.{d} He asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” And someone said, “Look, they are at Naioth in Ramah.”
He went there to Naioth in Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him also, and he went along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah.
He too stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel, and lay naked{e} all that day and all that night. Therefore they say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

notes.text: Hebrew teraphim, figurines of household gods, here apparently large enough to resemble a man. Likewise in verse 16.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “the liver of a goat” (Brenton), from a Hebrew word of similar form.
Naioth perhaps means “dwellings” or “pasture camps” (uncertain).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “the well of the threshing floor that is in Sephi” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “with only his undergarment.” The Hebrew word can mean partly clothed.

verses.text: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my guilt, and what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?”
He said to him, “Far from it! You shall not die. Look, my father does nothing great or small without disclosing it to me. Why should my father hide this matter from me? It is not so.”

But David swore again and said, “Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he says to himself, ‘Jonathan must not know of this, lest he be grieved.’ But truly, as Yahweh lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death.”
Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever your soul says, I will do for you.”
David said to Jonathan, “Look, tomorrow is the new moon,{a} and I ought to sit with the king to eat. But let me go, so that I may hide myself in the field until the third evening.
If your father misses me at all, say, ‘David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.’
Should he say, ‘Good,’ there is peace for your servant. But should his anger burn hot, be sure that harm has been settled on by him.
Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of Yahweh with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?”
Jonathan said, “Far be that from you! If I knew that harm had been determined by my father to come upon you, would I not tell you?”
Then David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan said to David, “Come, let us go out into the field.” And the two of them went out into the open field.

Jonathan said to David, “By Yahweh, the God of Israel!{b} When I have sounded out my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, and see that it is good toward David, will I not then send to you and uncover it in your ear?

But if my father has a mind to do you harm, Yahweh do so to Jonathan and more, unless I uncover it to you and send you off, so that you may go in peace. May Yahweh be with you, as he has been with my father.
If I am still alive, will you not show me the steadfast love{c} of Yahweh, so that I may not die?
Nor shall you cut off your steadfast love from my house, ever, not even when Yahweh cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth.”
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, “May Yahweh require it at the hand of David’s enemies.”{d}
Jonathan again made David swear, because of his love for him; for he loved him with the love of his own soul.
Then Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day go down quickly{e} and come to the place where you hid yourself on the day of the deed,{f} and remain beside the stone Ezel.{g}
And I will shoot three arrows to one side of it, as if I were shooting at a target.

Then I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, find the arrows.’ If I expressly say to the boy, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; take them,’ then come, for, as Yahweh lives, it is peace for you and there is nothing to fear.
But if I say to the lad, ‘See, the arrows are farther on from you,’ then go, for Yahweh has sent you away.
As for the matter of which you and I have spoken, look, Yahweh is between you and me forever.”
So David hid himself in the field. When the new moon came, the king sat down to eat the meal.
The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan stood up,{h} and Abner sat by Saul’s side, but David’s place was empty.
Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, “Something has happened to him; he is not clean. Surely he is not clean.”{i}
But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David’s place was empty. Saul said to Jonathan his son, “Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered Saul, “David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem.

He said, ‘Let me go, please, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the town, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away, please, and see my brothers.’ For this reason he has not come to the king’s table.”

Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse, rebellious woman!{j} Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
For all the days the son of Jesse lives on the ground, you will not be made firm, you or your kingship. Now send and fetch him to me, for he is a son of death.”{k}
Jonathan answered Saul his father, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”
But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father had determined to put David to death.
Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food on the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field at the time appointed with David, and a little boy with him.
He said to his boy, “Run, find the arrows I shoot.” As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
When the lad reached the spot where the arrow lay that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called out after the lad, “Is the arrow not farther on from you?”
Jonathan called after the boy, “Quick! Hurry! Do not stand still!” So Jonathan’s boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master.
The lad knew nothing of it; only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, “Go, carry them to the town.”

As soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the south side{l} and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. They kissed one another and wept with one another, until David wept the more.{m}

Then Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace, because we have both sworn in the name of Yahweh, saying, ‘Yahweh will be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.’” Then he rose and went away, and Jonathan went into the town.{n}

notes.text: The new moon marked the beginning of each month and was a festival day with special meals and sacrifices (Numbers 10:10; 28:11–15).
Hebrew “Yahweh, the God of Israel—” The oath formula is incomplete; a verb such as “is witness” may have been lost. This needs scholarly review.
Hebrew ḥesed, loyal love based on a covenant.
The Hebrew of verses 14–16 is difficult; “enemies of David” may be a scribal softening of “David” himself (compare 25:22).
Hebrew uncertain, literally “go down greatly.” The Septuagint reads “you shall stay three days” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “on the day of the business,” probably referring to the events of 19:2–7.
So the traditional Hebrew text; Ezel perhaps means “departure.” The Septuagint reads “beside that mound” (Brenton has “by that ergab”).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “and he went before Jonathan” (Brenton); some scholars suggest an original “Jonathan sat opposite.”
The Septuagint reads “because he has not purified himself” (Brenton) in place of the repeated clause.
Literally “son of a perverse woman of rebellion,” an insult aimed at Jonathan himself. The Septuagint reads “son of traitorous young women” (Brenton, modernized).
That is, he must die.
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “from the argab”), which reflects the mound of verse 19. The Hebrew reads “from beside the south.”
Hebrew uncertain.
In Hebrew the last sentence of this verse is 21:1, and 21:1–15 in English is 21:2–16 in Hebrew.

verses.text: David came to Nob,{a} to Ahimelech{b} the priest. Ahimelech came trembling to meet David and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no one with you?”

David told Ahimelech the priest, “The king gave me orders about a matter and told me, ‘Let no one know anything of the matter on which I send you and with which I have charged you.’ As for the young men, I have directed them to such and such a place.{c}
Now, what is there under your hand? Give five loaves of bread into my hand, or whatever is to be found.”
The priest answered David, “There is no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread, if only the young men have kept themselves from women.”

David answered the priest, “Indeed women have been kept from us, as before whenever I went out; the vessels{d} of the young men are holy even on a common journey. All the more today their vessels are holy!”{e}
So the priest gave him holy bread, for there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence,{f} which is removed from before Yahweh, to put hot bread in its place on the day it is taken away.
Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before Yahweh. His name was Doeg{g} the Edomite,{h} the chief of Saul’s herdsmen.
David said to Ahimelech, “Is there not here under your hand a spear or a sword? I did not even bring my sword or my weapons along, for the king’s errand was urgent.”

The priest said, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you will take that, take it, for there is no other but that here.” David said, “There is none like it; give it to me.”
David rose and fled that day from Saul and came to Achish{i} king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Is it not of him they sang in the dances, ‘Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”
David laid these words up in his heart and was greatly afraid before Achish, the king of Gath.
So he changed his behavior before them and acted like a madman in their hands. He made marks{j} on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down on his beard.
Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you see the man is insane. Why have you brought him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to act the madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?”

notes.text: In Hebrew, 20:42b is numbered 21:1, and 21:1–15 in English is 21:2–16 in Hebrew. Nob was a town of priests near Jerusalem (22:19).
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.” He is probably the same as Ahijah (14:3). Compare Mark 2:26, which names Abiathar.
The Hebrew phrase is deliberately vague (compare Ruth 4:1). The Septuagint reads “in the place called, The faithfulness of God, Phellani Maemoni” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “bodies.” The Hebrew word can mean equipment or the body.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Literally “bread of the face,” the twelve loaves set before Yahweh in the sanctuary each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9).
Doeg perhaps means “anxious” (uncertain).
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “the Syrian” (Brenton), a confusion of the similar Hebrew letters for Edom and Aram. The Septuagint also reads “tending the mules of Saul.”
The meaning of the name Achish is uncertain; it may be Philistine.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “drummed upon” (Brenton), from a Hebrew word of similar form.

verses.text: David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam.{a} When his brothers and all his father’s house heard of it, they went down there to him.
And every man in distress, and every man who had a creditor, and every man bitter of soul, assembled themselves to him, and he became captain over them. There were with him about four hundred men.
From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab.{b} He said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and my mother come out and stay with you, until I know what God will do for me.”
So he left them in the presence of the king of Moab,{c} and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold.
And Gad{d} the prophet spoke to David: “Abide not in the stronghold. Depart from here and enter into the land of Judah.” Then David went off and came into the forest of Hereth.

Saul heard that David and the men who were with him had been discovered. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him.

Saul said to his servants who stood about him, “Hear now, you Benjamites! Will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,

that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day.”
Then Doeg the Edomite, who was standing by the servants of Saul, answered, “I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
He inquired of Yahweh for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
Then the king sent to call Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and the whole house of his father, the priests that were in Nob; and they all came to the king.
Saul said, “Hear now, son of Ahitub.” He answered, “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul said to him, “For what reason have you two plotted against me, you and Jesse’s son, in that you gave him bread and a sword and sought God on his behalf, that he should rise up against me to lie in ambush, as at this day?”
Ahimelech answered the king and said, “And who among all your servants is faithful like David, the son-in-law of the king, who has charge of your guard,{e} and is honored in your house?

Is today the first time I have inquired of God for him? Far be it from me! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, little or much.”
The king said, “You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house.”

And the king said to the runners{f} who stood about him, “Turn and kill the priests of Yahweh, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me.” But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of Yahweh.
Then the king said to Doeg, “Turn yourself and fall on the priests.” And Doeg the Edomite turned and fell on the priests, and slew on that day eighty-five persons{g} wearing a linen ephod.
And Nob, the city of the priests, he struck with the edge of the sword, both man and woman, child and nursing infant, ox, donkey, and sheep, with the edge of the sword.
But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, named Abiathar,{h} escaped and fled after David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of Yahweh.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have brought about the death{i} of all the persons of your father’s house.
Stay with me; do not be afraid. For he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you will be safe.”

notes.text: Adullam was a town in the lowland of Judah, about 16 miles (26 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem. Its name perhaps means “refuge” (uncertain).
Mizpeh means “watchtower.”

So the Syriac and the Vulgate (reported). The Hebrew reads “he led them” (vocalized differently); the Septuagint reads “he persuaded the king of Moab” (Brenton, modernized). David’s great-grandmother Ruth was from Moab (Ruth 4:17).
Gad means “good fortune.”
The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “and turns aside to your obedience,” often understood as “captain over your bodyguard.” The Septuagint reads “executor of all your commands” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew ratsim, the king’s guard who ran before his chariot.
So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “three hundred and five men” (Brenton).
Abiathar means “the father is abundant” or “father of abundance” (uncertain).
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “I am guilty of the death”) and the Vulgate (reported). The Hebrew reads “I have turned against,” from a verb of similar form.

verses.text: Now they told David, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah{a} and are robbing the threshing floors.”
Therefore David inquired of Yahweh, “Shall I go and strike these Philistines?” Yahweh said to David, “Go and strike the Philistines and save Keilah.”
But David’s men said to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judah. How much more, then, if we go to Keilah against the ranks of the Philistines!”
So David inquired of Yahweh yet again. And Yahweh answered him, “Arise, go down to Keilah, for I am giving the Philistines into your hand.”
David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and drove away their livestock and struck them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.{b}
It was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, “God has handed him over{c} into my hand, for he is shut in, having entered into a city that has gates and bars.”
Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah to besiege David and his men.
David knew that Saul was devising harm against him. He said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
Then David said, “Yahweh, God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah to destroy the town on my account.
Will the citizens{d} of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? Yahweh, God of Israel, please tell your servant.” Yahweh said, “He will come down.”
Then David said, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?” Yahweh said, “They will surrender you.”

Then David and his men, about six hundred, rose up and went out of Keilah, and wandered wherever they might go. And it was told Saul that David had slipped away from Keilah, and he ceased from going out.
David dwelt in the wilderness in the strongholds, and he remained in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph.{e} Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.
David saw{f} that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.{g}
Then Jonathan the son of Saul arose and came to David at Horesh, and he made his hand strong in God.
He said to him, “Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father will not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you. Saul my father also knows this.”
The two of them made a covenant before Yahweh. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
Then the Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, “Does not David hide himself with us, in the strongholds in Horesh, in the hill of Hachilah, which lies on the south of Jeshimon?{h}
Now therefore, O king, come down according to all your heart’s desire to come down, and our part will be to surrender him into the king’s hand.”
Saul said, “May you be blessed by Yahweh, for you have had compassion on me.
Go, I pray you, and make ready still more. Learn and look at the place where he sets his foot, and who has seen him there, for it has been told me that he deals very craftily.

Look therefore, and learn all the hiding places where he hides himself, and return to me with the certainty of it.{i} Then I will go along with you; and if he is in the land, I will search him out through all the thousands of Judah.”
So they arose and went to Ziph before Saul. But David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon,{j} in the Arabah on the south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told, he went down to the rock{k} and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon.

Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain. And David was making haste to escape from before Saul, for Saul and his men were surrounding David and his men to take them.
Then a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid on the land.”
So Saul turned back from pursuing David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Divisions.{l}
David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi.{m}

notes.text: Keilah was a town in the lowland of Judah, about 3 miles (5 kilometers) south of Adullam.
The Septuagint reads “he went down with David to Keilah, having an ephod in his hand” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “alienated him”; the Hebrew verb usually means “estrange.” The Septuagint reads “sold him” (reported).
Or “lords” (Hebrew baʿale). Likewise in verse 12.
Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, about 4 miles (6 kilometers) southeast of Hebron.
Or “was afraid.” The Hebrew letters can be read either way.
Or “in the woods.” Horesh means “wood” or “thicket.”
Jeshimon means “wasteland,” the barren area west of the Dead Sea.
Or “at a set time.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Maon was a town about 8 miles (13 kilometers) south of Hebron.
Or “to Sela.”
Hebrew Sela-hammahlekoth, perhaps “Rock of Escape” or “Rock of Divisions” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “The divided Rock” (Brenton).
En-gedi means “spring of the young goat,” an oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea. In Hebrew this verse is 24:1, and 24:1–22 in English is 24:2–23 in Hebrew.

verses.text: When Saul came back from following the Philistines, he was told, “Look, David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.”{a}
Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Rocks of the Wild Goats.{b}
He came to the sheepfolds along the way, and a cave was there, and Saul went in to relieve himself.{c} Now David and his men were sitting in the far recesses of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Here is the day of which Yahweh said to you, ‘Look, I am giving your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it seems good to you.’” Then David arose and stealthily cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
Afterward David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.{d}
He said to his men, “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to put out my hand against him, for he is Yahweh’s anointed.”
So David held back his men with these words and did not let them rise against Saul. And Saul rose up from the cave and went on his way.
Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave and called after Saul, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David seeks your harm’?

Look, this day your eyes have seen how Yahweh gave you today into my hand in the cave. Some told me to kill you, but I{e} spared you. I said, ‘I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is Yahweh’s anointed.’

Moreover, my father, look, yes, look at the hem of your robe in my hand! Since I cut off the hem of your robe and killed you not, know and perceive that there is neither evil nor rebellion in my hand. I have not sinned against you, yet you hunt my soul to take it.
May Yahweh judge between me and you; may Yahweh avenge me on you; but my hand shall not be against you.
As the proverb of the ancients says, ‘Out of the wicked comes wickedness.’ But my hand shall not be against you.
After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom are you chasing? After a dead dog! After a single flea!
May Yahweh therefore be judge and decide between me and you, and see and plead my cause, and vindicate me against your hand.”{f}
And when David had made an end of speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.
He said to David, “You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, while I have repaid you evil.
You have declared this day how you have done good to me, for when Yahweh had shut me up into your hand, you did not kill me.
For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safely? So may Yahweh reward you with good for what you have done to me this day.
And now, look, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand.
Swear to me therefore by Yahweh that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father’s house.”
So David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.{g}

notes.text: In Hebrew, 24:1–22 is numbered 24:2–23 (see the note at 23:29).
Hebrew “the Rocks of the Ibexes” (wild mountain goats). The Septuagint reads “in front of Saddaeem” (Brenton, modernized), taking it as a place name.
Literally “to cover his feet,” a polite expression.
The Hebrew reads “Saul’s corner,” that is, the corner of his robe. Cutting the robe’s corner may have symbolized taking away his royal authority (compare 15:27–28).
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “I would not slay you, but spared you”) and other ancient witnesses. The Hebrew reads “but it spared you,” perhaps meaning “my eye spared you.”
Or “deliver me from your hand.”
The Septuagint reads “the stronghold of Messera” (Brenton), taking the Hebrew word for “stronghold” as a place name.

verses.text: Then Samuel died. All Israel assembled and lamented him, and they laid him in the grave at his house in Ramah. And David rose and went down into the wilderness of Paran.{a}
Now a man in Maon had his property in Carmel.{b} He was a very rich man, owning three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and he was at Carmel for the shearing of his sheep.
The man’s name was Nabal,{c} and his wife’s name was Abigail.{d} The woman was of good understanding and beautiful in form, but the man was harsh and evil in his dealings. He was a Calebite.{e}
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
So David sent ten young men, and David said to the young men, “Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Thus you shall say: ‘Long life to you!{f} Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have.
Now I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and nothing of theirs went missing all the days they were in Carmel.

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we have come on a good day.{g} Please give whatever your hand finds to your servants and to your son David.’”
When David’s young men came, they spoke to Nabal all these words in the name of David, and then they waited.
Nabal answered David’s servants, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? Many are the servants these days who are breaking away, each from his master.
Shall I then take my bread and my water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give it to men who come from I know not where?”
So David’s young men turned on their way and went back, and they came and told him all these words.

David said to his men, “Every man strap on his sword!” And every man strapped on his sword, and David also strapped on his sword. About four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred stayed with the baggage.
But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, “Look, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them.
Yet the men were very good to us, and we were not harmed, and we did not miss anything all the time we went about with them, when we were in the fields.
They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now therefore take thought and see what you will do, for evil is resolved against our master and against his whole household. He is so base a fellow{h} that no one can say a word to him.”

Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and about a bushel of roasted grain{i} and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go on before me; look, I am coming after you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
And as she was riding on the donkey, going down in the shelter of the hill, there came David and his men descending to meet her, and she encountered them.
Now David had said, “It was all for nothing that I kept watch over everything this man owns in the wilderness, so that not a thing of his was lost; and he has paid me back evil for good.
God do so to David,{j} and more also, if I let remain until daybreak a single male{k} out of all that are his.”
When Abigail caught sight of David, she quickly dismounted from the donkey and fell on her face before David and bowed to the ground.
Falling at his feet, she said, “Upon me, my lord, upon me let the iniquity rest. Let your handmaid, I pray, speak in your hearing, and listen to the words of your handmaid.

Let not my lord, I pray, regard this worthless man, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your handmaid did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent.

Now then, my lord, as Yahweh lives and as your soul lives, since Yahweh has held you back from coming into bloodguilt and from saving yourself by your own hand, now let your enemies and those who seek evil against my lord be as Nabal.
And now this gift{l} which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
Please forgive the trespass of your handmaid. For Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of Yahweh, and evil shall not be found in you all your days.

Should a man rise up to chase you and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord shall be bound up in the bundle of life{m} with Yahweh your God; but the souls of your enemies, them he will hurl away as out of the pocket of a sling.
And when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,

my lord shall have no cause of grief or stumbling of heart, either for having shed blood without cause or for my lord having saved himself. And when Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your handmaid.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!
Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from coming into bloodguilt and from saving myself with my own hand!

For as surely as Yahweh the God of Israel lives, who has kept me back from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there would not have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one male.”
Then David received from her hand what she had brought him, and he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. See, I have listened to your voice and have lifted up your face.”{n}

Then Abigail came to Nabal, and there he was, holding a banquet in his house like a king’s banquet. Nabal’s heart was glad within him, for he was exceedingly drunk; so she told him not a thing, small or great, until daybreak.
In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
About ten days later Yahweh struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has avenged the insult I received from the hand of Nabal, and has held back his servant from evil. Yahweh has brought back Nabal’s wickedness upon his own head.” And David sent word to Abigail, proposing to take her as his wife.
When David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they spoke to her, saying, “David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife.”
She arose and bowed with her face to the earth and said, “Look, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
Abigail hurried and arose and rode on a donkey, with her five young women who attended her. She went after the messengers of David and became his wife.
David had also taken Ahinoam from Jezreel,{o} and the two of them were wives to him.
Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti{p} son of Laish, who was of Gallim.

notes.text: So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Maon” (Brenton), as in verse 2.
This Carmel (meaning “garden land” or “orchard”) was a town in Judah near Maon, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) south of Hebron, not Mount Carmel in the north.
Nabal means “fool” (see verse 25). The word suggests a person who is morally senseless.
Abigail means “my father is joy” (uncertain).

Or “according to his heart”; the Hebrew letters can be read either way. Calebites were descendants of Caleb, who had received the region of Hebron (Joshua 14:13–14). The Septuagint reads “a man of a dog-like nature” (reported), playing on the name Caleb, which is similar to the word for “dog.”
The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “to the living one.”
A feast day, the time of sheep-shearing.
Hebrew “a son of Belial.” Likewise in verse 25.

Hebrew “five seahs,” about 33 quarts (37 liters); a seah was about a third of an ephah. The Septuagint reads “five ephahs of fine flour” and “one homer of dried grapes” (Brenton, modernized) instead of the hundred clusters.
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “So God do to David”). The Hebrew reads “to the enemies of David,” apparently a scribal change to avoid a curse falling on David himself.
Hebrew “one who urinates against a wall,” a coarse expression for a male. Likewise in verse 34.
Hebrew “blessing.”
An image of a person’s life kept safe like a precious thing tied in a bundle.
That is, “granted your request.”
Ahinoam means “my brother is pleasantness.” This Jezreel was a town in Judah (Joshua 15:56), not the northern city.
Called Paltiel in 2 Samuel 3:15. Palti means “my deliverance”; Paltiel means “God is my deliverance.” Gallim was a town near Gibeah (Isaiah 10:30).

verses.text: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, “Is David not concealing himself on the hill of Hachilah, which faces Jeshimon?”
So Saul rose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph, having with him three thousand picked men of Israel, to search for David in the wilderness of Ziph.
Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, which faces Jeshimon, beside the road. But David was staying in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul had come after him into the wilderness.
David therefore sent out spies and learned for certain that Saul had come.{a}

Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had camped. David saw where Saul was lying, and Abner son of Ner,{b} the captain of his host; Saul lay inside the camp ring,{c} and the troops were camped round about him.
Then David spoke up and said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai{d} son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul into the camp?” Abishai said, “I will go down with you.”
So David and Abishai came to the people by night, and there Saul lay sleeping inside the camp ring, his spear stuck in the earth at his head, and Abner and the people lying around him.
Then Abishai said to David, “God has shut up your enemy into your hand this day. Now let me pin him to the earth with the spear in one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice.”
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him. For who can put forth his hand against Yahweh’s anointed and be guiltless?”
David said further, “As Yahweh lives, Yahweh himself shall strike him: or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish.
Yahweh forbid that I should put forth my hand against Yahweh’s anointed. But now take, I pray, the spear that is at his head and the jug of water, and let us go.”

So David took the spear and the jug of water from beside Saul’s head, and they went away. No one saw it or knew it, nor did anyone wake, for all of them were asleep, because a deep sleep from Yahweh had fallen upon them.
Then David crossed over to the far side and stood on the top of the hill at a distance, with a wide space between them.
And David called out to the people and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you that call to the king?”

Then David said to Abner, “Are you not a valiant man? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord.

This thing that you have done is not good. As Yahweh lives, you deserve to die,{e} because you have not watched over your master, Yahweh’s anointed. And now look about: where is the king’s spear, and the jug of water that was at his head?”
Saul recognized David’s voice and said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” David said, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
And he said, “Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is in my hand?

Now therefore, I pray, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is Yahweh who has stirred you up against me, let him accept an offering;{f} but if it is the sons of men, cursed be they before Yahweh, for they have driven me out this day so that I have no share in the inheritance of Yahweh, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’
Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of Yahweh. For the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea,{g} as one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”

Then Saul said, “I have sinned. Come back, my son David, for I will no longer do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Look, I have acted the fool and have erred very greatly.”
David answered, “Here is the spear, O king!{h} Let one of the young men come over and fetch it.
Yahweh repays every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness. For Yahweh gave you into my hand today, but I would not put forth my hand against Yahweh’s anointed.
And see, just as your life was valued highly this day in my eyes, so may my life be valued highly in the eyes of Yahweh, and may he deliver me out of every distress.”
Then Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son David! You will both do great things and surely prevail.” So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.

notes.text: Or “had come to Nacon” (uncertain); the Hebrew word can be read as a place name.
Abner means “my father is a lamp” (uncertain). Ner means “lamp.”
Or “within the circle of wagons.” Likewise in verse 7.
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.” Abishai means “my father is a gift” (uncertain). Zeruiah, David’s sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), was mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.
Hebrew “you are sons of death.”
Literally “let him smell an offering,” that is, let him be appeased by a sacrifice.
The Septuagint reads “to seek your life” (reported) instead of “a single flea” (compare 24:14).
So the traditional Hebrew reading (qere). The written text (ketiv) reads “Here is the king’s spear.”

verses.text: David said in his heart, “Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than to escape quickly into the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will give up hope of me and seek me no more anywhere within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape from his hand.”
So David arose and crossed over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal’s widow.
When it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he sought him no more.

Then David said to Achish, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the country towns, that I may live there. For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?”
So Achish gave him Ziklag{a} that day. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
The number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.{b}

Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites,{c} and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as one goes to Shur and as far as the land of Egypt.
David would strike the land and leave neither man nor woman alive, and he would take the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the clothing, and come back to Achish.
When Achish asked, “Where have you raided today?” David would say, “Upon the south of Judah,” or “Upon the south country of the Jerahmeelites,” or “Upon the south country of the Kenites.”{d}

David left neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, “Lest they should report about us, saying, ‘So David has done.’” Such was his custom all the days he lived in the country of the Philistines.
And Achish trusted David, thinking, “He has made himself utterly odious to his people Israel; therefore he shall be my servant forever.”

notes.text: Ziklag was a town in the Negeb, in the south of Judah; its exact location is uncertain.
Hebrew “days and four months”; “days” here means a year. The Septuagint reads “four months” (reported).
So the traditional written text (ketiv); the margin reads “Gezrites.” Some Septuagint manuscripts lack this name (reported).
Hebrew “the Negeb,” meaning “dry land,” the southern region of Judah.

verses.text: In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, “Know for certain that you shall go out with me in the army, you and your men.”
David answered Achish, “So be it; you shall learn what your servant will do.” And Achish replied to David, “So be it; I will make you keeper of my head{a} for all time.”
Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had lamented him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had driven out of the land those who called up the dead and those who consulted spirits.{b}
So the Philistines were gathered together, and they came and pitched at Shunem;{c} and Saul assembled all Israel, and they pitched at Gilboa.{d}
When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
When Saul inquired of Yahweh, Yahweh did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.
Then Saul said to his servants, “Seek out for me a woman who is a medium,{e} that I may go to her and inquire of her.” His servants said to him, “Look, there is a woman who is a medium at En-dor.”{f}

So Saul disguised himself and put on other clothes and went, he and two men with him. They came to the woman by night. And he said, “Divine for me, I pray, by the spirit, and bring up for me the one whom I shall name to you.”

The woman said to him, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off from the land those who call up the dead and those who consult spirits. Why then do you set a trap for my life, to have me put to death?”
But Saul swore to her by Yahweh, “As Yahweh lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing.”
Then the woman asked, “Whom am I to bring up to you?” He answered, “Samuel; bring him up to me.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman spoke to Saul, saying, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king said to her, “Do not be afraid. What do you see?” And the woman said to Saul, “I see a god{g} coming up out of the earth.”
He said to her, “What form has he?” She said, “An aged man is coming up, covered with a mantle.” Then Saul perceived that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and did homage.

Then Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you troubled me, to bring me up?” Saul said, “I am sorely distressed. The Philistines wage war against me, and God has departed from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called you to make known to me what I should do.”
Samuel said, “Why then do you ask me, since Yahweh has turned away from you and has become your adversary?{h}
Yahweh has done to you{i} just as he spoke by me. Yahweh has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, to David.
Because you did not listen to the voice of Yahweh, nor execute the heat of his anger upon Amalek, for that reason Yahweh has done this thing to you this day.

Moreover, Yahweh will also give Israel along with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Yahweh will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines.”
Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground and was greatly afraid because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all day and all night.

The woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was badly shaken, she said to him, “Look, your handmaid has listened to your voice, and I have put my life in my hand and have obeyed the words you spoke to me.
Now therefore, I pray, you also listen to the voice of your handmaid. Let me set a morsel of bread before you, and eat, so that you may have strength when you go on your way.”
He refused and said, “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, pressed him, and he listened to their voice. So he rose from the ground and sat on the bed.
Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she hurried and slaughtered it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread from it.
She set it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.

notes.text: That is, “my bodyguard.”
Hebrew ʾovot and yiddeʿonim, those who claimed to consult the spirits of the dead. Likewise in verse 9.
Shunem was a town in the territory of Issachar, on the slope of the hill of Moreh.
Gilboa was a mountain ridge south of the Jezreel Valley.
Hebrew “a woman who is mistress of a spirit” (baʿalat ʾov).
En-dor means “spring of the dwelling” (uncertain), a town north of the hill of Moreh.
Or “a godlike being” or “divine beings” (Hebrew ʾelohim, with a plural verb). The Septuagint reads “gods ascending out of the earth” (Brenton).
The Hebrew word ʿar is uncertain; perhaps “adversary” (an Aramaic sense). The Septuagint reads “is with your neighbor” (reported).
So many Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (reported); the traditional text reads “to him,” that is, to David.

verses.text: Now the Philistines gathered all their forces to Aphek,{a} while Israel was camped by the spring that is in Jezreel.
Now the lords of the Philistines were marching past by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were marching past at the rear with Achish.

Then the princes of the Philistines said, “What are these Hebrews here for?” And Achish answered the princes of the Philistines, “Is not this David, servant of Saul the king of Israel, who has been with me these days, or these years? I have found no fault in him from the day he went over to me until this day.”

But the princes of the Philistines were angry with him and said to him, “Make the man go back, so that he returns to his place that you appointed him. He shall not go down with us to the battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary{b} to us. For with what could this man win back the goodwill of his lord? Would it not be with the heads of these men here?
Is not this the David of whom they answered one another in the dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”

Then Achish called David and said to him, “As Yahweh lives,{c} you have been upright, and it seems good to me that your going out and your coming in with me in the army should be so, for I have found no evil in you from the day of your coming to me until this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not look on you with favor.
So now turn back and go in peace, that you may not do evil in the eyes of the lords of the Philistines.”

David said to Achish, “But what have I done? And what have you found in your servant from the day that I came before you until this day, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered David, “I know that you are as good in my eyes as a messenger{d} of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, ‘He shall not go up with us to the battle.’
Now then, rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you;{e} and as soon as you are up early in the morning and have light, depart.”
So David set out early, he and his men, to leave in the morning and return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

notes.text: Aphek was a town in the Sharon plain, the gathering place before the battle of 4:1.
Hebrew satan, “adversary.”
