A Philistine king swearing by Yahweh may reflect courtesy toward David.
Or “angel.”
The Septuagint adds “and go to the place where I appointed you, and entertain no evil thought in your heart, for you are good in my sight” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: Now it came to pass, when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had made a raid on the Negeb and on Ziklag. They had overthrown Ziklag and burned it with fire,
and had taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way.
When David and his men came to the town, there it was, burned with fire, and their wives and their sons and their daughters taken captive.
Then David and the people who were with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep.
David’s two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the widow of Nabal the Carmelite.

And David was in great straits, for the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was bitter, each man for his sons and for his daughters. But David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, son of Ahimelech, “Bring the ephod here to me, I pray.” So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David inquired of Yahweh, “Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?” He answered him, “Pursue, for you shall surely overtake them and shall surely rescue.”
So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor,{a} where those who were left behind stayed.
But David pursued, he and four hundred men, while two hundred stayed behind who were too faint to cross the brook Besor.
They found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him bread, and he ate, and they gave him water to drink.
They also gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. When he had eaten, his spirit came back to him, for he had eaten no bread and drunk no water for three days and three nights.
David said to him, “Whose are you? And from where do you come?” He said, “I am an Egyptian lad, a slave of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me three days ago, because I fell ill.
We made a raid on the Negeb of the Cherethites{b} and on that which belongs to Judah and on the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire.”
David said to him, “Will you bring me down to this band?” He said, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will bring you down to this band.”

When he had brought him down, look, they were scattered over the face of all the land, eating and drinking and feasting, on account of the vast plunder they had seized out of the Philistines’ land and out of Judah’s land.
And David smote them from the dusk until the evening of the following day,{c} and not one man of them escaped except four hundred young men who mounted camels and fled.
David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.
There was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither plunder nor anything they had seized. All of it David brought back.
David also took all the flocks and the herds, which they drove before those other livestock, and they said, “This is David’s spoil.”{d}

Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too faint to follow David, whom they had left at the brook Besor. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him. When David came near to the people, he greeted them.

Then answered all the evil men and the base fellows{e} among the men who had gone with David, and said, “Since they went not with us, we will give them nothing of the plunder that we have rescued, but only to every man his wife and his children, that they may lead them away and go.”
But David said, “You shall not do so, my brothers, with that which Yahweh has given to us, who has kept us safe and has delivered the raiding band that came upon us into our hand.
And who will hearken to you in this matter? For as his portion is that goes down to the battle, so shall his portion be that remains with the baggage. They shall share alike.”
And from that day forward he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel, to this day.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah, his friends, saying, “Here is a gift{f} for you from the spoil of the enemies of Yahweh.”
He sent to them in Bethel, and to them in Ramoth of the south, and to them in Jattir,
and to them in Aroer, and to them in Siphmoth, and to them in Eshtemoa,
and to them in Racal, and to them in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to them in the cities of the Kenites,
and to them in Hormah, and to them in Bor-ashan,{g} and to them in Athach,
and to them in Hebron, and to every place where David himself and his men had been accustomed to go.

notes.text: Besor was a stream (a wadi) south of Ziklag, flowing west to the Mediterranean.
The Cherethites were a people related to the Philistines, perhaps from Crete. Some of them later served in David’s bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18).
The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “from the twilight until the evening of their morrow.”
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Hebrew “men of Belial.”
Hebrew “blessing.”
So many Hebrew manuscripts (reported); others read “Cor-ashan.” Bor-ashan means “smoking pit.”

verses.text: Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines pursued hard after Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua,{a} the sons of Saul.
The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers, the men with bows, found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.{b}

Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and run me through and make sport of me.” But his armor-bearer would not, for he was greatly afraid. So Saul took the sword and fell upon it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his own sword and died with him.
So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on that same day together.

When the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent them round about the land of the Philistines, to proclaim the tidings in the temples of their idols and among the people.
They put his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth,{c} and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.{d}
But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. They came to Jabesh and burned them there.{e}
And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.

notes.text: Abinadab means “my father is generous.” Malchi-shua means “my king is salvation” (uncertain).
Or “he was greatly afraid of the archers.” The Septuagint reads “he was wounded under the ribs” (Brenton, modernized).
The plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess. The Septuagint reads “the temple of Astarte” (Brenton). First Chronicles 10:10 adds that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
Beth-shan means “house of quiet” (uncertain), a city at the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys.
Burning the bodies was not the usual Israelite practice. Some have reported that the verb here may mean “anointed with spices” (scholarly review). First Chronicles 10:12 does not mention the burning.
